issue.title: Name the class of an evaluated expression after the element that declares it, rather than numbering it
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

The classes generated for the evaluated expressions of a class were numbered (`$Foo$Expr0`, `$Foo$Expr1`, ...) by `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter`, a static map that is never cleared. In a JVM that keeps the processors' classes loaded between compilations, as a build tool's daemon does and as development mode will (the next pull request in this stack), a class compiled again gets new names: `$Foo$Expr1` instead of `$Foo$Expr0`. A new name is a class added and another removed, so development mode restarts the application where it could redefine the class in place, and compiling the changed source alone first (later in this stack) finds an output it does not have.

Numbers also depend on which sources a compilation holds. An expression is named after the class that declares the annotated element, so when `Bar extends Foo` compiles without `Foo`, the members `Bar` inherits number `$Foo$Expr<n>` from 0 and can overwrite a class `Foo`'s compilation wrote for another expression (constructors are not inherited, so the numbering shifts). `Foo`'s definition then evaluates the wrong expression.

## The fix

An expression class is named after what declares it, rather than numbered: the class declaring the annotated element, the element, the annotation and its member, and a hash.

```
test.$Foo$Expr$field$b$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$constructor$param0$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$method$find$param1$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$type$Requires$condition$<hash>
```

- Each language describes the element (`getExpressionElementName`, a new internal hook of `AbstractAnnotationMetadataBuilder`): `type`, `field$<name>`, `property$<name>` (Kotlin, Groovy, Python), `getter$<name>` and `setter$<name>` (Kotlin), `component$<name>` (Java records), `method$<name>`, `constructor`, and a parameter by its index (`$param<n>`), which a class file keeps when it has no parameter names. Python, which always compiles from source, names a parameter.
- A Kotlin accessor and a setter's parameter belonged to `java.lang.Object` until now, since `getClassDeclaration` does not resolve them. Their expressions are now named in the class declaring the property.
- The hash, the first 64 bits of SHA-256 as 16 hexadecimal digits, covers the erased parameter types of a method or constructor, the annotation's package and the expression, so overloads, annotations of the same simple name and repeated annotations get names of their own, and a class of a given name holds the expression it was named for.
- Characters that cannot be in a Java name become `_`. A name longer than 200 bytes in UTF-8 is cut short before the hash, and so is the class's own name when it leaves no room.
- An element a language does not describe, such as an annotated type argument, is numbered as before, and `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter` stays for that and for other modules that number their own expressions.

The name no longer depends on the other sources of the compilation or on the order elements are visited, so the classes need no reset between compilations.

When the annotated element is read from a class file (`isReadFromClassFile`, the other new hook), the compilation of its class wrote the expression class. `EvaluatedExpressionProcessor` then looks the class up and does not write it again when it is found. A subclass compiled on its own neither rewrites nor takes over the classes of its superclass. A superclass compiled by a version that numbered its expression classes has none of that name, and the subclass writes them as before. An element of a source of the compilation is always written, so a stale class file on the class path is never trusted.

Editing an expression changes its hash, so its class is renamed. Compiling a class whose expressions did not change keeps their names.

## In the stack

It touches no file of #14331, #14332 or #14333 and could land on its own on 5.3.x; #14337 relies on it.

## Tests

- `EvaluatedExpressionClassNamesSpec` (new, core-processor): the format, what goes into the hash, arrays whose values would join to the same text, expressions whose 32-bit hashes collide, replaced characters, and names cut short for long ASCII and CJK class and element names.
- `ExpressionClassNamesSpec` (inject-java):
  - the names of a field, a constructor parameter and a method parameter;
  - the same names when a class is compiled twice in one JVM;
  - distinct names for overloads with the same expression and for repeated `@Property` annotations, and 250-character and 100-CJK-character field names cut short to 200 bytes;
  - `Foo`, with an expression on a constructor parameter and one on a field, compiled on its own, then `Bar extends Foo` compiled on its own against `Foo`'s class files: `Bar`'s output holds no `$Foo$Expr` class, and both beans get the right values. Without the class-path lookup, this test fails;
  - with `Foo`'s expression classes removed, as from an older compilation, `Bar` writes the one it inherits.
- The Java and Groovy test helpers `AbstractEvaluatedExpressionsSpec` find the classes by name, not by the counter. The Kotlin `MethodArgumentEvaluationContextExpressionsSpec` checks the name of a function's expression class.
- Ran: `:micronaut-core-processor:test` (38), `:micronaut-inject-java:test` (6393, 10 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-groovy:test` (1342, 14 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-kotlin:test` (1111, 9 skipped), `:test-suite-jdt:test` (87, javac and JDT name the classes the same), and the `io.micronaut.docs.expressions` tests of `test-suite`, `test-suite-groovy` and `test-suite-kotlin`; none failed. `:test-suite-python:compileTestPython` compiles the Python expression docs with the new names; the Python test tasks were skipped in this build. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on every touched module (only the 6 TODO warnings already there).
- Codex review, five rounds: names bounded by bytes rather than characters, Kotlin accessors, array values encoded unambiguously, long class names, and a 64-bit hash instead of 32 bits, all fixed. The fifth round found nothing.

comment.body:
## Re-review of the rewrite (head 87497d2c29)

Thanks for the rewrite. My original concern is resolved. Names now depend only on the declaring class, the element, the annotation, the member and the expression. Encoding uses UTF-8 and `Locale.ROOT`, and nothing depends on visit order or on which sources a compilation holds. So `Bar`'s compilation names `Foo`'s expression exactly as `Foo`'s did and can't overwrite it with something else. Definitions reference the class by name, so definitions built by older versions keep working at runtime. Collisions and truncation are well tested in `EvaluatedExpressionClassNamesSpec`.

1. **Subclasses now depend on synthetic classes inside the superclass's jar** (`EvaluatedExpressionProcessor.build()` / `isOnClasspath`). When the annotated element comes from a class file and a class with that name is found, `Bar` doesn't write its own copy, so `Bar$Definition` refers to `$Foo$Expr$field$b$…$<hash>` in `Foo`'s jar. Before, `Bar` always carried its own copy.

   Failure scenario: an application is compiled against version 1.0 of a library whose `Foo` has `@Value("#{…}")` on an inherited field. Version 1.0.1 changes the expression, or is rebuilt with a Micronaut that names these classes differently, numbered or a future scheme. With 1.0.1 on the runtime classpath, the application fails with `NoClassDefFoundError` when it builds `Bar`'s metadata. Before, it ran, at worst evaluating the old expression.

   Since names are now content-addressed, always writing the class is safe from the original bug. A copy can only ever hold the same expression as the original, so the cost is identical duplicate classes, split across jars. Otherwise the naming scheme (format, hash input, each language's element strings) becomes a binary contract between library versions, which should at least be documented.

2. **The numbered fallback still has the original collision** (`AbstractAnnotationMetadataBuilder` around lines 971-978). Elements a language doesn't describe still use the static counter and never consult `isReadFromClassFile`. Examples: the `default -> null` kinds in Java, and Kotlin type arguments and references, or a `KSValueParameter` whose parent is neither a setter nor a function. For those, `Bar` compiled without `Foo` can still write a different `$X$Expr0`. It's rare, but the description presents the problem as gone.

3. **`READ_FROM_CLASS_FILES` is static and cleared by any compilation's `finish()`.** Take two compilations that overlap in one loader, the case the earlier commits were written for. One reads `Foo` from a class file and adds it, while the other compiles `Foo` from source. If there's a stale copy in the output, `Foo`'s own compilation can then skip writing its class. It needs both overlap and a stale output, so it's low.

4. **Tests:** the class-file and fallback cases are only tested for Java. Kotlin (`*_LIB` origins), Groovy (non-primary `ClassNode`) and Python have no test of a subclass compiled against class files, and Kotlin getter/setter naming has no test either.

Minor:
- Names can reach about 206 bytes once `.class` is added, which is over eCryptfs's 143-byte limit.
- A Kotlin class extending a javac-compiled class never matches the existing name (`field$x` vs `property$x`, `int` vs `kotlin.Int`), so it always writes its own copy. That's harmless.

issue.title: Development mode: credit a Kotlin source the build compiled with the classes its SourceFile names, so that its first edit compiles their dependents
issue.body:
The first edit of a Kotlin source the build compiled could compile it alone and serve stale code.

`SourceIndex` knows a source the launcher has not compiled yet only by its path, which names one class: `util/Constants.kt` names `util.Constants`. Kotlin files often don't match that:
- a file of top-level declarations compiles to `ConstantsKt`;
- a file may declare several classes, or none named after it;
- a file's package need not be its directory's.

On the first edit of such a file:
- its real classes were neither hidden nor replaced;
- their dependents were not found;
- a constant it declares was not seen.

In a Kotlin petclinic, a first edit of a `const val` in `Constants.kt` compiled one source and was never served.

Now a Kotlin source with no record is credited with the top-level classes in the output whose `SourceFile` attribute names it:
- Only the package directory the source declares is read.
- That package is read past comments, a shebang, a byte order mark and file annotations, with names in backticks or outside ASCII. `KotlinCompilation.credit` now uses the same parser.
- Two sources of one package and file name under different roots are credited with neither's classes.

### Tests
In `KotlinSourceCompilerSpec`, with the source mapping deleted as if the build had compiled everything:
- an edit of a `const val` in a file outside its package's directory compiles the reader that inlined it, which then serves the new value;
- a file of two classes that drops one compiles that class's user, which then fails against it.

Both fail without the change. Also added: a table of package directives.

Checks on the branch: `:micronaut-dev:test`, `:micronaut-dev-tck:test`, `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` pass.

### Codex review (gpt-5.6-sol, medium)
Fixed:
- the package is read from the source, not from its directory;
- commented-out package lines are ignored;
- blanks inside a backticked name are kept;
- CR-only line ends are handled.

The last fix (CR line ends) was not reviewed again. Open:
- **Multi-file facades (`@file:JvmMultifileClass`, P1).** A part's facade is not credited to every part's source, so the first edit of one part does not compile the facade's dependents. Compiling one part alone is a limitation of the dev compiler for multi-file classes generally, not of this index; not addressed here.
- **Top-level class names containing `$`.** A class such as `` `A$B` ``, or a file with `$` in its name, is taken for a nested class and not credited.

issue.title: Read the defaults of an annotation no source of the round uses off its compiled class in Kotlin
issue.body:
KSP resolves an annotation's member defaults from a usage of the annotation (`KSAnnotation.defaultArguments`). `KotlinAnnotationMetadataBuilder` finds that usage with `Resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation`, which answers from the files of the current round only, and in an incremental KSP run those are the changed files.

An annotation that a visitor adds by type, such as micronaut-data's `@Query` on derived finder methods, therefore got its defaults only when a changed file happened to use it.
- When none did, incremental builds wrote `registerAnnotationType(Query)` into the regenerated repository definitions instead of `registerAnnotationDefaults(Query, {nativeQuery=false, readOnly=true})`. This happened in Gradle's KSP as well as in development mode's embedded KSP.
- Their bytes then differed from a clean build's, and in development mode such a reload restarts the application instead of redefining classes.
- A clean build of a project that never uses `@Query` explicitly lacked the defaults too.

When no usage is found, the defaults are now read off the annotation's compiled class, if it can be loaded, in the same shapes and order as a usage's defaults:
- a class value is converted through the declaration KSP resolves a usage's class literal to, so it is named exactly as a usage names it. A primitive class is named after its wrapper (`int.class` → `java.lang.Integer`), an object array class `java.lang.Object[]`, a primitive array class `int[]`, and `void.class` `kotlin.Unit`. Javac names the first two `int` and `[Ljava.lang.String;`. Making the usage path as accurate would change the metadata existing Kotlin builds generate for any annotation using such a class, so that is left for a separate change;
- enum values become the constant's name;
- arrays become a `List`.

These cases keep the previous behaviour, defaults only when a file of the round uses the annotation:
- an annotation declared in the project's sources, whose class cannot be loaded from the processor path. Its defaults can still differ between incremental and clean builds;
- an annotation whose class cannot be read;
- an annotation whose class on the processor path has other members than the declaration KSP sees (another version on the compile classpath), rather than caching part of the defaults for the whole JVM. A version that differs only in default values or member types is not told apart;
- an annotation with a member defaulting to a nested annotation, since a usage's nested annotation holds only the members it writes.

**Release note:** clean builds of projects that never use an annotation such as `@Query` explicitly now register its defaults, so their generated classes differ from the previous release's.

### Tests
- New cases in `AnnotationMemberDefaultsSpec`:
  - A visitor adds a test annotation with defaults of every kind by type, including `String[].class`, `int.class`, `int[].class`, `Integer.class` and `void.class`, and no source uses it. It checks the added annotation value's defaults, `VisitorContext.getAnnotationDefaultValues` and the generated definition's registered defaults. The same compilation with a source using the annotation must give the same values in the same shapes and order. It fails without the change (no defaults).
  - The sources declare an annotation again with a member its class on the processor path lacks: no defaults are read off the class. It fails without the member check.
- Run with `--tests` filters: `io.micronaut.kotlin.processing.annotations.*`, `io.micronaut.kotlin.processing.visitor.*`, `*MyRepo3Spec` and `*IntroductionAdviceSpec`, 250 tests, 0 failures, 1 skipped as before. The full inject-kotlin suite was not run locally.
- `:micronaut-inject-kotlin:spotlessCheck` passes. `checkstyleMain` has no Java sources in this module.
- Reproduced before the change with plain Gradle KSP, Kotlin 2.4.10, KSP 2.3.12 and micronaut-data-processor 5.2.4: an incremental build after editing only a repository without explicit `@Query` regenerated its definition without the defaults. With the change, the incremental KSP output is identical to a clean build's.

### Codex review (gpt-5.6-sol, medium)
- First pass, both fixed: partial defaults were cached when a member defaulted to a nested annotation; a linkage error while reflecting could fail the compilation.
- Second pass: no findings.
- After review: fixed `void.class` defaults dropping every default, and a processor-path class with extra members. Not handled: a version whose members have the same names but other types (above).

Open, not handled:
- The nested-annotation case has no test.

## Follow-up: point 3 tested

I ran the specs locally on this branch (JDK 25): `AnnotationMemberDefaultsSpec` (3/3) and `NestedAnnotationDefaultsSpec` (1/1) pass.

To check point 3, I added a scratch spec in the same style as the new test. A Java annotation with these two defaults is added by a visitor, and its defaults are read once with no source using it and once with a source using it:

```java
Class<?> arrayClass() default String[].class;
Class<?> primitiveClass() default int.class;
```

The two compilations disagree:

| Default | No usage (compiled class) | With a usage (KSP) |
|---|---|---|
| `String[].class` | `[Ljava.lang.String;` | `java.lang.Object[]` |

issue.title: Development mode: inject the LiveReload script into @View pages and other pages a body writer renders
issue.body:
Part of the development-mode reloading plan, micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654.

## Problem

Under `mnDev` and `mn:dev`, LiveReload's script was never injected into `@View` pages, so a browser showing a view did not reload on a change. Plain HTML pages, `String` or `byte[]` bodies and static files did get it.

## Cause

`LiveReloadScriptFilter` injects only into a body that is already text: a `CharSequence`, `byte[]` or a static file.

A view is not text yet when the filter sees it:
- Views' `ResponseBodySwapperFilter` replaces the controller's model with a `ModelAndView` and sets `text/html`.
- `RawModelAndViewMessageBodyHandler` renders the template into the response's stream when the response is written, after the filters.
- The filter therefore saw a `ModelAndView` and returned at its last `else`.

The same applies to any body a writer renders, such as a `Writable`. A route that only declares `produces = "text/html"` also has no content type at filter time, because the server sets it when it writes the response.

This was first read from the code, then confirmed by the new test, which fails without the fix: the `/view` page was served without the script. Views needs no change.

## Fix (development only)

When LiveReload injects its script and the response is HTML, the filter now does two new things:
- It renders a body of any other type with the writer the server would use for it, found in the `MessageBodyHandlerRegistry` by the body's class and the response's type. The render runs within the request's `ServerRequestContext`, as views' `writeTo` expects. The page goes out as rendered, with the script, so it is not rendered a second time.
- It takes the type a route produces when the response has none and the route produces exactly one. A route producing several negotiates as it writes, and is left alone.

A rendered page without a body end, or one the script must not go into, is sent byte for byte as its writer wrote it, with the writer's own type and no charset added. The writer writes against a copy of the headers. The response takes that copy only once the writer has finished, so a writer that gives up partway leaves the response as it was.

The response to a HEAD request is handled as the one to a GET: the body the route executor moved aside is handled, then put back aside. HEAD therefore gets the `Content-Length` of the page with the script and `Cache-Control: no-store`, as GET does.

The body end is found case-insensitively in the page itself, not in a lower-case copy, which can be longer than the page (`İ` becomes two characters).

### Content-Security-Policy

A page that declares a policy is left without the script, which the policy could block. Before this PR the filter already left alone a response with a `Content-Security-Policy` header, or with a policy in a `<meta http-equiv>` element. It now also covers:
- a writer that sets the header while it renders: the page is sent as rendered, without the script
- a policy added by a `ResponseHeaderPopulator`: the filter now runs ahead of `ResponseHeaderPopulatorFilter`, so it handles the response after that filter. Both had `FIRST.before()`, which left their order to how the beans were found.

The filter now runs at `ServerFilterPhase.FIRST.before() - 1`, ahead of the built-in phases and of views' filter, so it sees the response after them. A filter ordered ahead of it, such as one at `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE`, still sees the response after it.

Unchanged:
- With LiveReload off the filter returns at its first check, as before.
- A response that is not HTML (JSON, a CSS file) is untouched.
- The registry is resolved through a `BeanProvider` on the first page rendered.
- The filter is development-only, as before.

A blocking writer, such as views, now renders on the thread that runs the response filter rather than the one the server would choose for the write. This happens only in development mode with LiveReload on.

## Tests

`LiveReloadRenderedPageTest` (new, `micronaut-dev-livereload`) launches an application with:
- a model swapped for a page by a response filter and rendered by a blocking `MessageBodyWriter`, as views does
- a `Writable` route that produces `text/html`
- a JSON route and a CSS file
- writers that change their own headers while writing: one that sets an ISO-8859-1 charset, one that marks its output `text/plain`, one that sets a policy, and one that sets a header and then gives up with `UnsupportedOperationException`
- a writer emitting ISO-8859-1 with no charset and no body end

It checks that the pages carry the script with a matching `Content-Length` and `no-store`, and that HEAD gets the same length, type and cache header as GET. It also checks that the JSON, the CSS and the page without a body end are byte for byte as written, and that a header from a writer that gave up does not reach the response. It fails without the fix on `/view`. The HEAD, no-body-end and gave-up cases fail on the commit before review.

`LiveReloadScriptFilterTest` covers a page with `İ` before the body end.

`:micronaut-dev-livereload:test`, `:micronaut-dev:test --tests 'io.micronaut.dev.http.*'`, and `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on both modules pass.

## End to end

Java petclinic through `./gradlew mnDev` and `mvn mn:dev` on H2, with the sample's own build files and the jars of the earlier end-to-end test (core with #14275, #14307, #14328, #14329 and #14330; the plugin, module and serde #1500 PRs of that test, views #1212 and #1233 among them).

| Path | Without this PR, Gradle and Maven | With this PR, Gradle and Maven |
|---|---|---|
| `/vets`, `/vets/html` (`@View`, JTE) | no script | script, `Content-Length` of the page with it, `Cache-Control: no-store` |
| `/vets/json` | untouched | untouched, `application/json`, no cache header |
| `/resources/css/petclinic.css` | untouched | byte for byte the same, its own cache header |

The pages still carried the script after body, route, view, message and model edits, including after restarts. A first version without the filter order worked under Gradle but not under Maven: the views filter and this one had the same order, and the classpath decided which handled the response first. The order now makes the result independent of that.

## Codex

- Round 1:
  - A blocking writer ran on the event loop. Fixed: it now renders on the blocking executor, and the test's writer fails on an event loop.
  - A writer the response carries was ignored. Fixed: it is chosen as the server chooses it.
- Round 2: an `InputStream`, `File` or `ByteBody` HTML body turned into a 500, because its writer only writes through the server's response path. Fixed: such bodies are skipped, and the test covers a streamed page.
- Round 3: a writer that sets `Content-Encoding` while writing would be spliced into. Fixed: the page goes out as written.
- Round 4: the charset or type a writer sets while writing was ignored. Fixed: the page is decoded and sent with them.
- Round 5: a writer that marks its output as something other than HTML would be spliced into. Fixed: that output goes out as written.
- Round 6: a writer that sets a `Content-Security-Policy` while rendering still got the script. Fixed, and the test covers it; it failed before.
- Round 7: this filter and the response-header populator had the same order, so a policy the populator added might not be seen. Fixed by ordering this filter one ahead. A unit test of the order fails before; the end-to-end populator case passed either way, since the tie happened to fall the right way.
- Round 8 reports that a null stage from a `@ResponseFilter` declared to return `CompletionStage` is rejected. It is not: that check applies only to filters registered as functions (`RouteFunctionFilter`). An annotated method marked `@Nullable` may return null, and the JSON, CSS and synchronous HTML cases in the tests and on petclinic all ran through it.
- Rounds 4 and 5 are now covered by end-to-end tests of writers that change their headers while writing. Round 3, a writer that sets `Content-Encoding`, still has no end-to-end test. The petclinic e2e above ran before the round 5 change and was not rerun after review.
- After review: no findings.

issue.title: Development mode: serve an edited message bundle without a restart
issue.body:
Part of the development-mode reloading plan, micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654.

## Problem

Under `mnDev` and `mn:dev`, an edit to a message bundle (`messages*.properties`) was not served until the next restart. Nothing in the log said why. The development-mode guide says a changed message bundle reaches the beans that watch resources of its kind, but nothing watched them.

## Cause

- The build tools type the whole of `src/main/resources` as the configuration root. A bundle there is reported as a resource change of that root, and only a configuration file refreshes the configuration, so the change reached the resource watches and stopped there.
- No watch took it. The bundle is cached in three places:
  - `ResourceBundleMessageSource`'s message cache
  - its bundle cache, and its default bundle
  - the JDK's `ResourceBundle` cache, per class loader
- The generation's class loader reads the edited file live. But a generation keeps its loader, so the JDK cache kept the bundle it had already loaded.

## Fix (development only)

- `DevMessageBundles` is a `@Context` bean in `micronaut-dev`, active only in development mode. It watches the `.properties` files of every resource root (a `views` or `static` root nested in the configuration root takes the files under it). On a change, it:
  - clears the JDK's `ResourceBundle` cache of the generation's loader, whether or not the context has a message source, so code that calls `ResourceBundle.getBundle` itself (a view engine's resolver, user code) reads the edit too;
  - calls a new `@Internal` method, `ResourceBundleMessageSource.reload()`, on every `ResourceBundleMessageSource` the context created, of any scope. It records them as a `BeanCreatedEventListener<MessageSource>`, weakly, since a factory method may declare only `MessageSource`.
- `reload()` clears the JDK's cache for the source's class loaders, loads the default bundle again, and clears both caches. It runs with the generation's loader as the context loader.
- A source created with `new` rather than as a bean keeps its own caches; only the JDK's cache is cleared for it.
- The source is refreshed in place rather than recreated. Recreating it would destroy the composite message source and, through it, the server's HTML error response provider and the server, which stops the application. #14341 turns that into a restart; refreshing in place costs nothing.

Production behaviour does not change:
- Nothing calls `reload()` outside development mode.
- `getRawMessage` and the default lookup read the default bundle field once each, into a local, so a reload that empties it between two reads cannot fail a lookup. No synchronisation is added.
- The default bundle field is no longer `final`, since `reload()` replaces it. It is a plain field, not volatile, and nothing orders a lookup's read of it with the replacement: a lookup on another thread may use the previous bundle until it sees the write. The second reload 250 ms later drops what such a lookup cached, but nothing guarantees it is the last. The field's Javadoc says so.

## Tests

`MessageBundleReloadTest` (new, `micronaut-dev`) launches an application, edits `messages.properties` and then `messages_de.properties`, and checks each edit is served, with no restart and the same generation. Two cases:
- a controller reading a singleton and a `@Prototype` `ResourceBundleMessageSource("i18n.messages")`;
- a controller calling `ResourceBundle.getBundle` itself, with no message source bean.

Each fails without its part of the fix (`expected <200 hello-2> but was <200 hello-1>`): the first without the fix, or for the prototype with only the context's singletons reloaded; the second without the clearing of the generation loader's cache. With the fix, each edit is served within about a second.

`ResourceBundleMessageSourceReloadTest` (new, `micronaut-inject`) checks that `reload()` reads an edited bundle, and that a deleted default bundle leaves lookups empty.

Also run, all passing:
- `ConfigurationStalenessTest`, `DevRuntimeTest`
- after review: the whole `micronaut-dev` suite (458 tests, 1 skipped, 0 failures), and `micronaut-inject` `io.micronaut.context.i18n.*`
- test-suite `io.micronaut.context.i18n.*` and `io.micronaut.docs.i18n.*`
- `CompositeMessageSourceTest` (before review)
- `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-inject` and `micronaut-dev`

## End to end

The end-to-end numbers below predate the review changes; they were not measured again.

Java petclinic through `./gradlew mnDev` and `mvn mn:dev` on H2, with the sample's own build files and the jars of the earlier end-to-end test (core with #14275, #14307, #14328, #14329 and #14330; the plugin, module and serde #1500 PRs of that test). The edit changes `vet.ourVeterinarians` in `src/main/resources/i18n/messages.properties`, which the plugins type as the `i18n` root; the check is the heading of `/vets`.

| | Gradle | Maven |
|---|---|---|
| Without this PR | not served within 10 s (served only after a later restart) | the same |
| With this PR | served in 196–225 ms (median 207 ms, n=9) | 198–236 ms (median 212 ms, n=5) |

There was no restart and no new generation; the log shows `Message bundles read again: 1 message source(s) for 1 changed file(s)`. Edits made after the delayed second reload had emptied the caches were served in 6–15 ms, before the watcher fired, because the next lookup read the file. Body, route, view and model edits interleaved with these behaved as without this PR. The load average was 3 to 13. A view edit takes about 210 ms both with and without this PR.

## Codex

- First round: a lookup in flight across `reload()` can put back a value it read before the clear. This is fixed by a second reload 250 ms later, which keeps every lookup unsynchronised.
- Second round, the same point again: a lookup in flight for more than 250 ms, or one reading `defaultBundle` without a happens-before, could still keep a stale message until the next edit. Closing that completely would need a volatile field or a lock on `getRawMessage`, a production lookup path, which development-mode changes must not touch. It stays as described in `reload()`'s Javadoc.
- After review, three more: `defaultBundle` read twice could be emptied between the reads (fixed, read once); prototype-scoped sources were missed (fixed, every created source is recorded); bundles under nested `views` or `static` roots were not watched (fixed, every root is watched). The volatile point came up again and stays as above.

issue.title: Warm up GraalPy beside the launch of a Python application in development mode
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654: the first launch of a Python application in development mode. Does not depend on #14308; the saving is the same on GraalPy 25.4.4 and 25.5.5.

## What was going on

The closed #14304 looked as if creating an `Engine` early on the launch thread saved about 540 ms of the first launch. It didn't: that build also started a thread that built a whole Python context, and that context is the saving. The later build that seemed to lose the saving by moving the lookup off the launch thread had also deferred that thread until the application had started.

| Each alone, petclinic on 25.5.5, JVM start to `Startup completed`, medians of 5 | ms |
|---|---|
| Nothing | 4028 |
| An `Engine` on the launch thread | 4047 |
| An `Engine` on another thread | 3977 |
| A context on another thread, started as the context is configured | 3469 |

The three builds of #14304 on 25.4.4, 6 launches each: nothing 4254, engine on the launch thread with the background context 3554, no such engine with the background context 3541, background context deferred until started 4150.

## The cause

The first context of a JVM spends most of its time loading and initializing GraalPy's classes, about 10,000 of them, on the thread that starts the application. That is once per JVM, and the launch does other work for about a second before it gets there, so another thread can do it in that time.

- No context is needed for the effect: on another thread, only `Class.forName` over the same class list gives 3686 ms without initializing, and 3400 ms with, against 4058 ms with nothing and 3528 ms with a context.
- It is real work moved to another core, not work avoided: the same context on the launch thread first gives 4161 ms.
- The lead is what counts. A context started as the application's own starts saves nothing (4062 ms against 4092 ms): the application thread's CPU in its context falls from 2054 to 1475 ms, but its wall time stays at about 2100 ms, because the two threads wait for each other. Started when the context is configured, 3542 ms; at the start of `MicronautDevMain.launch`, 3281 ms against 4086 ms; from a `-javaagent` premain, 3107 ms.

`TruffleCompilerThread` stays at one thread with this. An `Engine` alone not helping also rules out language or option discovery and the context class loader of the first engine.

## The fix

`MicronautDevMain.launch` starts `PythonWarmUp`: a daemon thread that initializes a GraalPy context and closes it. Only a launch with Python sources starts it, or in test mode one with Python tests, on a JVM, with the Python runtime on the classpath and `micronaut.python.enabled` not false as a system property or environment variable. `micronaut.dev.python.warm-up=false` turns it off. Nothing is added at runtime call sites, and without a development runtime nothing changes.

## Measurements

The same jars in both columns, only `micronaut.dev.python.warm-up` differs, alternating, 8 launches each, medians, load average 3–5. CPU is the JVM's at `Startup completed`, then 1.5–3 s later.

| | Off | On | Saved | CPU at ready | CPU later |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| petclinic, 25.5.5 | 4039 ms | 3239 ms | 800 ms | 13.07 → 14.08 s | 15.39 → 15.63 s |
| petclinic, 25.4.4 | 4258 ms | 3389 ms | 869 ms | 14.16 → 15.08 s | 17.21 → 18.01 s |
| simple-python, 25.5.5 | 2714 ms | 2260 ms | 454 ms | 8.50 → 9.71 s | 11.50 → 12.76 s |
| simple-python, 25.4.4 | 2759 ms | 2285 ms | 474 ms | 8.71 → 9.94 s | 12.16 → 13.73 s |

The first request after ready doesn't change (petclinic 574 and 582 ms), so nothing is deferred to it.

Through the real `pyronaut dev` on petclinic and 25.5.5, 6 launches each: JVM start to ready 4186 → 3385 ms, the command to ready about 16.3 → 15.6 s. Reloads and the request after them are the same: 2526 and 2556 ms, 149 and 149 ms, 24 edits each.

With 12 busy loops beside it, load average 13–15: 6761 → 6098 ms. Held to the efficiency cores with `taskpolicy -c background`, 4 launches each: 27.2 → 23.5 s.

To have the two threads meet at different points, 90 launches started a probe context with the same options at a random delay up to 1.3 s, with no hang. That makes a class initialization deadlock unlikely, not impossible. With this change, a launch from an empty GraalPy resource cache works, 4 times out of 4.

## What it doesn't do

- **Configuration files.** It runs before the application's configuration is read, so `micronaut.python.enabled: false` in `application.yml` isn't seen. An application with Python sources that turns Python off that way pays the CPU of the warm-up, and nothing else changes.
- **`engine.CompilerThreads`.** The first engine of the JVM sizes the compiler queue (checked with thread dumps: 3 configured gave 3 without this, and 1 with it), and without the option the warm-up would give the default 4. An application that configures more than one gets one in development mode unless it turns the warm-up off. The guide says so.
- **Production.** A context started the same way also saves in `pyronaut run` on a JVM (petclinic 3916 → 3335 ms, simple-python 2687 → 2336 ms). This is left out on purpose: production must honour the two settings above and can't read them this early, and a production JVM can use the AOT cache below instead, though that was measured on the development launch only.

The AOT cache `tool.pyronaut.toolchain.aot-cache` already offers does the same job far better, and shows how much of this is class loading: the same petclinic development launch with a cache takes 1655 ms against 4086 ms in a separate series, CPU 7.56 s against 13 s, after a 12 s training launch. With a cache, a context started this way saves about another 150 ms (1504 ms). Reloads with a cache weren't measured.

## Tests

New `PythonWarmUpTest` in `test-suite-dev-python`: a Python launch warms up on a daemon thread with the launcher's loader and writes nothing, and a context works after it; Python tests warm up in test mode only; no Python sources, no runtime on the classpath, Python switched off and the off switch all start nothing.

Ran with `-Ppython-ci`: all of `:test-suite-dev-python:test` (22 tests, on the commit before the test mode addition), `PythonWarmUpTest` on the final commit, and all of `:micronaut-dev:test`, whose classpath has no polyglot. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-dev`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `test-suite-dev-python`; `micronaut-dev` has no enabled `checkstyleTest`. One run of `:micronaut-dev:test` beside other heavy work failed `DevRequestAdmissionTest` with a 403; it passed alone and in the next full run.

Not run: Windows, Linux, a native image, a machine with one or two CPUs, `pyronaut test -t` end to end. The measurements used this change laid over the jars of the test environment rather than a full build of this branch.

issue.title: Upgrade GraalPy and GraalVM to 25.5.5.0.3
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Moves GraalPy and GraalVM from 25.4.4.1.1 to 25.5.5.0.3, whose `python-resources` jar ships bytecode for the standard library. It had none before, so every GraalPy context compiled each standard library module it imported.

## What changed

- `managed-graal` and `managed-graalpy` in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`
- `graalVersion` and `graalpyVersion` in `gradle.properties`
- `version: '25.5'` for `setup-graalvm` in `python.yml` and `python-static-compilation.yml`. Oracle's download service lists "Oracle GraalVM 25 Innovation 5 25.5.5.0.3", and the action's version match accepts `25.5` for it
- the examples in `pythonRuntime.adoc`

`crema.yml` is left alone: it pins its own Oracle GraalVM for the Crema tests. Nothing else in the repository names the version.

## To decide before this leaves draft

- `python.yml` says it is synced from `micronaut-project-template`, whose `master` still has `version: '25.4'`. A sync would put it back, and the JDK would then no longer match the artifacts, so Python would run interpreted. The template needs the same change.
- `graalVersion` only feeds the docs, including `sdk install java {graalVersion}-graal`. SDKMAN lists Oracle GraalVM up to 25.4.4.1+1 today, so that command won't work until 25.5 is listed. `25.5.5+1` follows the old value's form and is a guess at the identifier.

## Is the shipped bytecode used?

Yes, checked on the embedding path as `GraalPyContextFactory` builds a context, with Oracle GraalVM 25.5.5.0.3 on the JVM:

- `sys.implementation.cache_tag` is `graalpy253-313`, the tag on the shipped files, as it is on 25.4.4. The magic number does change, `52530d0a` to `66530d0a`.
- All 681 shipped `.pyc` have flags 3: hash-based and checked. So extracting them, which changes modification times, doesn't invalidate them.
- `GraalPyResources` sets `python.CheckHashPycsMode=never`, so the hash isn't even computed. A plain context uses `default`; the hash there matched the source.
- With `python.VerboseFlag`, 69 code objects came from `.pyc` and 0 from source, in both a plain context and the virtual file system configuration.

The standalone launcher, a native image, also loaded `json` from `.pyc`. A native image of an application was not built.

## Measurements

Petclinic in restart mode on H2. Both lines use the same core and Pyronaut commits apart from the version, each with its own matching Oracle GraalVM JDK. 30 edits per series, first 10 discarded, medians of the other 20. The series alternate. CPU is per edit and includes about 3 s idle. `#14303` is lazy asyncio.

The cleanest round, load average 3–5:

| | reload | first request | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25.4.4 + #14303 | 1134 ms | 160 ms | 4.55 s |
| 25.5.5 without #14303 | 1090 ms | 161 ms | 4.13 s |
| 25.5.5 + #14303 | 1105 ms | 112 ms | 4.01 s |

Two earlier rounds ran at load 6–30 and are much noisier: reload 1172–1806 ms for 25.5.5 + #14303, against 1346–1564 ms for 25.4.4 + #14303, first request 113–214 ms against 194–210 ms. Differences of 50 ms in reload can't be told from noise here.

## Size

`python-resources` grows from 14.1 MB to 27.9 MB, and the extracted GraalPy home from 22 MB to 71 MB.

## Tests

With Oracle GraalVM 25.5.5.0.3 as `JAVA_HOME`, `./gradlew pythonCheck -Ppython-ci --continue`: every test passes except `NettyPythonEventLoopSemanticsTest.serverBindsEveryAddressOfAName`, which fails on macOS regardless of this change. `:micronaut-inject-python:compileVfsPythonBytecode` runs on the new JDK. That run was before the commit that only changes docs. No Java or Python source changed, so checkstyle and spotless have nothing new to look at and were not run.

Not run: Linux, Windows, this repository's CI (a draft runs none), `crema.yml`, a native image of an application, and tests outside `pythonCheck`.

issue.title: Keep the running generation in development mode while a configuration file cannot be read, and never exit the launcher over one
issue.body:
Part of #13654. Dev mode stays running after a failure and tries again on the next change, so the error can be corrected. A configuration file that could not be read lost the pool and, on the next start, could end the JVM.

## What was wrong

On petclinic in restart mode, with the Pyronaut command line kept out of the way, a syntax error in `application.toml`:

1. Failed the refresh, which restarted the application. The pool was released and Oracle went to 0 sessions, for a file no new generation could read either.
2. Failed the start of that generation in `Micronaut.start()`, which called `System.exit(1)`. The JVM stayed up about 30 s while its shutdown hook ran, then was gone.

## Cause

- `ConfigurationStaleness.refreshConfiguration` turned any failure of the refresh into "restart instead". A failed read leaves the environment as it was (`refreshProperties` publishes atomically), so there was no need.
- `Micronaut.mayExit` asks the environment whether it is in development mode. An environment that failed to read its files has published no properties, so it answers no, and the launcher exits. The setting `DevApplicationContextConfigurer` gave it is still among its property sources.

## The fix

- **The running generation carries on.** A refresh that fails, and whose environment can't be refreshed on its own either, gives `ConfigurationStaleness.UNREADABLE`. `DevRuntime` logs the error with what the parser says, leaves the generation running, and holds the batch as it holds one that failed to compile. Once the file is corrected, what waited is applied: a file put back as it was changes nothing.
- **The launcher no longer exits.** `Micronaut.isExitAllowed` also checks the environment's property sources for development mode, the one with the highest order deciding. This is reached only when `isDevelopmentMode()` says no, so a production start that fails exits as before.

The check in `DevRuntime` runs only when a configuration file changed. Nothing changes on any runtime path.

## Not changed

- A restart that was asked for still restarts, and a generation that already failed still tries a start, which fails until the file is corrected. The launcher stays up in both. In the second case the retained beans are released once the file is edited, as #14293 documents.
- A resource delivered in the same batch as the unreadable file is delivered again when the batch comes back. It needs a static file edited in the same batch; the batch has to be kept so that a later class change doesn't start a generation that can't read the file.

## Tests

In `DevRuntimeTest`. Each of the four failed before the change it covers:

| Test | Without the change |
|---|---|
| `aConfigurationFileThatCannotBeReadLeavesTheGenerationRunningUntilItIsCorrected` | Fails: a new generation |
| `aConfigurationFileCorrectedAsItWasLeavesTheGenerationAsItIs` | Fails: a new generation |
| `aStartThatCannotReadItsConfigurationLeavesTheLauncherUp` | The test JVM exits with 1 |
| `sourcesThatFailedToCompileStillWaitAfterAConfigurationFileThatCannotBeRead` | Fails: the first edit is lost |

- `:micronaut-dev:test`: passed in full before the last two commits (property order, sources kept). On the final code it had one failure, `whileNoGenerationRunsAConnectionIsAnswered503UntilAServerTakesTheSocketsBack`, whose client reached an SSH server on the port it had picked (`SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.9`). It passes alone. `DevRuntimeTest` passes on the final code.
- `MicronautDevelopmentModeSpec` and `TrainingRunTest` in `:micronaut-context:test` pass.
- `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-dev`, `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-context` pass.

End to end, with micronaut-projects/pyronaut#418, on petclinic with Oracle in restart mode: a syntax error in `application.toml`, then the fix, then an edit. Same JVM, Oracle container, pool identity and 2 sessions throughout, and requests kept answering 200.

Not run: YAML end to end (`DevRuntimeTest` uses JSON, since the TOML loader isn't in this repository), and the native toolchain.

issue.title: Name the class of an evaluated expression after the element that declares it, rather than numbering it
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

The classes generated for the evaluated expressions of a class were numbered (`$Foo$Expr0`, `$Foo$Expr1`, ...) by `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter`, a static map that is never cleared. In a JVM that keeps the processors' classes loaded between compilations, as a build tool's daemon does and as development mode will (the next pull request in this stack), a class compiled again gets new names: `$Foo$Expr1` instead of `$Foo$Expr0`. A new name is a class added and another removed, so development mode restarts the application where it could redefine the class in place, and compiling the changed source alone first (later in this stack) finds an output it does not have.

Numbers also depend on which sources a compilation holds. An expression is named after the class that declares the annotated element, so when `Bar extends Foo` compiles without `Foo`, the members `Bar` inherits number `$Foo$Expr<n>` from 0 and can overwrite a class `Foo`'s compilation wrote for another expression (constructors are not inherited, so the numbering shifts). `Foo`'s definition then evaluates the wrong expression.

## The fix

An expression class is named after what declares it, rather than numbered: the class declaring the annotated element, the element, the annotation and its member, and a hash.

```
test.$Foo$Expr$field$b$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$constructor$param0$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$method$find$param1$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$type$Requires$condition$<hash>
```

- Each language describes the element (`getExpressionElementName`, a new internal hook of `AbstractAnnotationMetadataBuilder`): `type`, `field$<name>`, `property$<name>` (Kotlin, Groovy, Python), `getter$<name>` and `setter$<name>` (Kotlin), `component$<name>` (Java records), `method$<name>`, `constructor`, and a parameter by its index (`$param<n>`), which a class file keeps when it has no parameter names. Python, which always compiles from source, names a parameter.
- A Kotlin accessor and a setter's parameter belonged to `java.lang.Object` until now, since `getClassDeclaration` does not resolve them. Their expressions are now named in the class declaring the property.
- The hash, the first 64 bits of SHA-256 as 16 hexadecimal digits, covers the erased parameter types of a method or constructor, the annotation's package and the expression, so overloads, annotations of the same simple name and repeated annotations get names of their own, and a class of a given name holds the expression it was named for.
- Characters that cannot be in a Java name become `_`. A name longer than 200 bytes in UTF-8 is cut short before the hash, and so is the class's own name when it leaves no room.
- An element a language does not describe, such as an annotated type argument, is numbered as before, and `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter` stays for that and for other modules that number their own expressions.

The name no longer depends on the other sources of the compilation or on the order elements are visited, so the classes need no reset between compilations.

When the annotated element is read from a class file (`isReadFromClassFile`, the other new hook), the compilation of its class wrote the expression class. `EvaluatedExpressionProcessor` then looks the class up and does not write it again when it is found. A subclass compiled on its own neither rewrites nor takes over the classes of its superclass. A superclass compiled by a version that numbered its expression classes has none of that name, and the subclass writes them as before. An element of a source of the compilation is always written, so a stale class file on the class path is never trusted.

Editing an expression changes its hash, so its class is renamed. Compiling a class whose expressions did not change keeps their names.

## In the stack

It touches no file of #14331, #14332 or #14333 and could land on its own on 5.3.x; #14337 relies on it.

## Tests

- `EvaluatedExpressionClassNamesSpec` (new, core-processor): the format, what goes into the hash, arrays whose values would join to the same text, expressions whose 32-bit hashes collide, replaced characters, and names cut short for long ASCII and CJK class and element names.
- `ExpressionClassNamesSpec` (inject-java):
  - the names of a field, a constructor parameter and a method parameter;
  - the same names when a class is compiled twice in one JVM;
  - distinct names for overloads with the same expression and for repeated `@Property` annotations, and 250-character and 100-CJK-character field names cut short to 200 bytes;
  - `Foo`, with an expression on a constructor parameter and one on a field, compiled on its own, then `Bar extends Foo` compiled on its own against `Foo`'s class files: `Bar`'s output holds no `$Foo$Expr` class, and both beans get the right values. Without the class-path lookup, this test fails;
  - with `Foo`'s expression classes removed, as from an older compilation, `Bar` writes the one it inherits.
- The Java and Groovy test helpers `AbstractEvaluatedExpressionsSpec` find the classes by name, not by the counter. The Kotlin `MethodArgumentEvaluationContextExpressionsSpec` checks the name of a function's expression class.
- Ran: `:micronaut-core-processor:test` (38), `:micronaut-inject-java:test` (6393, 10 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-groovy:test` (1342, 14 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-kotlin:test` (1111, 9 skipped), `:test-suite-jdt:test` (87, javac and JDT name the classes the same), and the `io.micronaut.docs.expressions` tests of `test-suite`, `test-suite-groovy` and `test-suite-kotlin`; none failed. `:test-suite-python:compileTestPython` compiles the Python expression docs with the new names; the Python test tasks were skipped in this build. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on every touched module (only the 6 TODO warnings already there).
- Codex review, five rounds: names bounded by bytes rather than characters, Kotlin accessors, array values encoded unambiguously, long class names, and a 64-bit hash instead of 32 bits, all fixed. The fifth round found nothing.

comment.body: Probaly the best solution would be $field$fieldName $method$name$param1 etc naming to prevent conflicts or to make sure the expression counter for the class is not being reset

issue.title: Development mode: compile an edit of Kotlin method bodies with kotlinc alone, keeping what KSP produced
issue.body:
In development mode, an edit of method bodies in a Kotlin source now compiles with kotlinc alone and keeps what the symbol processors produced. KSP was 65 to 80% of every Kotlin compile.

### What changes
**The body-edit path.** When a changed source qualifies, it compiles first with kotlinc alone (`KotlinCompilation.runWithoutProcessors`), without its dependents. Only the source's own classes are hidden from that compilation: what the processors generated for it stays on its classpath, so a source that uses a class generated from it compiles, and a generated top-level function stays listed in the module metadata. If every class compiled differs from the output's in method bodies only (compared as `DependentStructure` from #14338 does, so the line numbers of a static initializer do not count, its code does), the outputs the processors produced for the source before are staged again unchanged: generated classes, `META-INF/micronaut` entries, resources and generated sources. KSP does not run. Otherwise the normal compile with KSP and the dependents follows, and its diagnostics are the ones reported.

A changed source qualifies when all of these hold:
- the request is incremental, deletes nothing and has no sibling output;
- it compiled earlier in this session;
- its "declaration text" is the same as at that compile;
- none of its classes is inlined into another class (the SMAP, from the PR below);
- its last edit did not change its structure (below).

**Declaration text.** The class file does not show what the processors read of a source's text, so `KotlinDeclarationText` scans for it: the package and import directives, the KDoc comments, and every annotation with its arguments, including `SOURCE` retention ones. It is a token scanner that skips strings, characters, templates, comments and labels; it is not a parser, so anything extra it picks up only sends an edit through the processors. The text is recorded from what was read before each successful compile; on the body-edit path, the text that was checked is the one recorded, so an edit saved after the check goes through the processors next.

**When the recorded texts are dropped.** If the processor path, the options, the compile classpath, the size or time of a jar on either, or any file of a class directory on either (another project's output) changes, the recorded texts are forgotten. Directories are stamped by walking them, and only for a compiler that records texts. The first edit of each source in a session therefore goes through the processors.

**Structure-change heuristic** (as #14338 does for javac's changed-first). A source whose last compile changed its structure, or whose body-edit attempt was rejected, compiles with the processors at once on its next edit, so a structural edit does not pay for a failed kotlinc-alone attempt each time. A later compile with the processors that changes bodies only clears the mark. A compiler that records no text (javac, Groovy) never takes this path.

**Off switch.** The system property `micronaut.dev.compile.body-edits-without-processors=false` on the development JVM compiles every edit with the processors. It is documented in the dev-mode guide next to `micronaut.dev.compile.retain-processors`.

### Measurements
Kotlin petclinic (data-jdbc, serde, validation, security, views-jte; KSP 2.3.12, Kotlin 2.4.10) under Gradle `mnDev`. Median edit-to-served time in ms, p90 in brackets, CPU of the dev JVM per edit. Load is the 1-minute load average; the machine is shared.

The two builds:
- **before:** #14340's top plus the first PR of this stack.
- **after:** this stack.

Both had #14341 and #14307 merged locally and the same plugin and modules. They alternated, so load fell alike on each.

**Body edits only** (n=5 per kind, load median 8 before and 10 after):

| Edit | before | after | CPU before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| body (controller) | 1177 (1310), restart | 583 (600), redefine | 3918 → 1091 |
| dtobody (data class) | 1401 (1632), 3 sources | 518 (551), 1 source | 3946 → 829 |
| service | 1256 (1281) | 557 (609) | 2915 → 1014 |
| top (top-level function) | 1519 (1756), restart | 460 (478), redefine | 4605 → 626 |

**Mixed series**, 14 kinds interleaved per round (n=6, load median 11 for both). The after column includes the other PRs of this stack:

| Edit | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| service | 1468 | 562 |
| modelbody (entity body) | 3163, restart, 11 sources | 500, redefine, 1 source |
| constbody | 1262 | 516 |
| companion | 5668, restart, 32 sources | 546, redefine |
| internal | 2097, restart | 563, redefine |
| top | 2222, restart | 510, redefine |
| inline | not served | 1806, redefine, 5 sources |
| const | 5232 | 3887 |
| route | 1380 | 1342 |
| dataprop | 1554 | 1914 |
| entity | 3267 | 2778 |
| newctl | 1281 | 1055 |
| body | 1109 | 1270 |
| dtobody | 2077 | 1562 |

In the mixed series, `body` and `dtobody` always follow a structural edit of the same file (`route` and `dataprop`), so the heuristic sends them through KSP. A structural edit that follows a body edit pays the failed kotlinc-alone attempt: `dataprop` is about 350 ms slower.

**Outputs.** After 13 incremental edits, the session's output was compared with a clean Gradle build of the edited sources:
- 139 of 145 entries identical;
- 6 repository definitions differ, from the round-dependent `@Query` defaults fixed in #14357 on 5.2.x;
- with #14357 cherry-picked locally, 145 of 145 identical.

**Functional checks** (compile error and fix, failed start, deletes, rapid edits, in-flight requests, templates, static files, broken YAML, availability under a request every 200 ms) pass as before. The exception is "data written survives a restart", which the sample's `CREATE_DROP` schema fails.

### Tests
- `KotlinSourceCompilerSpec`:
  - a body edit compiles one source without the processors and keeps their generated class byte for byte;
  - a KDoc change, and a change to a `SOURCE` retention annotation's argument, go through the processors;
  - the first edit after the session starts goes through the processors, and the next one does not;
  - a structural edit and the edit after it go through the processors, and the one after that does not;
  - changed processor options go through the processors;
  - an inline function's second body edit still compiles its callers.
  - a source calling the class and the top-level function generated from it compiles without the processors edit after edit;
  - a new source calls a generated top-level function after a body edit (the module metadata still lists its facade);
  - a body edit that moves the lines of a companion object's and a top-level property's static initializer takes the path;
  - documentation saved after the check goes through the processors with the next compile;
  - a changed file in a class directory of the compile classpath sends the next edit through the processors;
  - the off switch.
- `KotlinDeclarationTextTest`: what the scanner records, and that a body change leaves it equal.
- The processor tests fail without the change. The existing incremental test now makes its base class edit structural, since a body edit no longer compiles dependents.

Checks on the branch: `:micronaut-dev:test`, `:micronaut-dev-tck:test`, `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` pass (`:micronaut-dev:test` and the checks again after the review fixes; `:micronaut-dev-tck:test` was not run again). The measurements were taken on the branch before it merged the latest #14340 top; that merge brought #14340's own review fix and 5.3.x changes.

### Codex review (gpt-5.6-sol, medium)
Fixed:
- imports and package in the text;
- annotation arguments after a blank;
- imports after a semicolon;
- processor and classpath configuration changes, including jars rebuilt in place;

issue.title: Never fail on an originating element without a native element, and let a Python type-use view provide its declaration's
issue.body:
## The bug

`AnnotationProcessingOutputVisitor.toNativeOriginatingElements` cast every originating element to `ElementProvider` unchecked. `visitMetaInfFile`, `visitGeneratedFile` and `visitGeneratedSourceFile` use it.

In Python processing, the type of a field or the return type of a method that carries type-use annotation metadata, such as `color: Color | None`, is a `TypeAnnotatedClassElement`, or a `TypeAnnotatedEnumElement` for an enum. Neither implements `ElementProvider`. A visitor that passed one as the originating element of a META-INF file failed:

```
ClassCastException: TypeAnnotatedEnumElement cannot be cast to ElementProvider
  at AnnotationProcessingOutputVisitor.visitMetaInfFile
  at JavaVisitorContext.visitMetaInfFile
  at PythonVisitorContext.visitMetaInfFile
```

This was found through micronaut-projects/micronaut-openapi#2879, where the OpenAPI visitor crashed on the Python docs example. That PR works around it by passing the declaration.

`visitServiceDescriptor` checked the type with `instanceof`, but then passed `null` to the `Filer`. javac's `Filer` (checked on JDK 25) looks up the file of each originating element and fails with a `NullPointerException` on `null` (`JavacElements.getFileObjectOf`, called from `JavacFiler.originatingFiles`). So a service descriptor with an element that provides no native element failed as well.

## The fix

1. `TypeAnnotatedClassElement` implements `ElementProvider` and returns the native element of the class element it wraps, or `null` if that element provides none. A type-use view of a class then credits a file to its declaration's source, as the unwrapped class element does. Incremental compilation relies on that crediting.
2. `toNativeOriginatingElements` leaves out an element that is not an `ElementProvider` and any `null` native element, so the output visitor never throws on an element it can't map. `visitServiceDescriptor` now uses it as well. `visitClass` already checked the native type.

This is compile-time code only.

## Tests

- `TypeAnnotatedClassElementTest` (inject-python): the field types and the method return type, an enum among them, are type-annotated wrappers that provide the originating element of the wrapped class element. It fails without part 1.
- `PyronautCompilerIncrementalTest.tracksFilesOriginatingFromTypeAnnotatedTypesIncrementally`: an isolating visitor writes a META-INF file for each field type and method return type, with that type as the originating element. The types are a Python enum, a Python class and `str`, each `| None`. The files are written and credited to their source. An unrelated edit leaves the other source's file alone, and deleting the source removes its files. It fails with the `ClassCastException` without the fix. With only part 2 it passes, because Pyronaut's compiler also credits Python processing outputs to the source being processed. The unit test above covers part 1.
- `JavaVisitorContextSpec` (inject-java): a META-INF file whose originating elements include a `ReflectClassElement`, and a service descriptor with one. Without the fix the first fails with the `ClassCastException` and the second with javac's `NullPointerException`.

inject-python's tests now depend on `jackson-annotations`, because the Java stub of a Python enum carries `@JsonValue`.

## Not covered here

`PythonParameterElement`, `PythonPropertyParameterElement` and `PythonEnumConstantElement` don't implement `ElementProvider` either. Passing one no longer fails, but the file isn't credited to a source.

## Review notes left open

Codex (gpt-5.6-sol, medium) raised one point, which this PR leaves as is:

- *Preserve Python origins for wrapped Java-backed types.* For `str | None`, the wrapper forwards the native element of `java.lang.String`, a classpath declaration that maps to no source. The point is that the file should be credited to the Python source that uses the type. This PR keeps the wrapper consistent with the unwrapped type: an unannotated `str` already credits `java.lang.String`. Crediting a type use to the source that uses it would change behaviour for every element, not only this wrapper. In Pyronaut's incremental compiler the file is still credited to the Python source and removed with it; the incremental test covers `str | None` too.

## Review

Looks good:
- `toNativeOriginatingElements` now leaves out elements it can't map instead of failing on the cast.
- `visitServiceDescriptor` goes through the same path, so javac's `Filer` no longer receives a `null` originating element.
- `TypeAnnotatedClassElement` passes through its declaration's native element, wrapped wrappers included.
- Making it an `ElementProvider` changes nothing else: the only other check for one in main code, in `PythonStubGenerator`, looks for a field element, which this wrapper never returns.

issue.title: Warm up GraalPy beside the launch of a Python application in development mode
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654: the first launch of a Python application in development mode. Does not depend on #14308; the saving is the same on GraalPy 25.4.4 and 25.5.5.

## What was going on

The closed #14304 looked as if creating an `Engine` early on the launch thread saved about 540 ms of the first launch. It didn't: that build also started a thread that built a whole Python context, and that context is the saving. The later build that seemed to lose the saving by moving the lookup off the launch thread had also deferred that thread until the application had started.

| Each alone, petclinic on 25.5.5, JVM start to `Startup completed`, medians of 5 | ms |
|---|---|
| Nothing | 4028 |
| An `Engine` on the launch thread | 4047 |
| An `Engine` on another thread | 3977 |
| A context on another thread, started as the context is configured | 3469 |

The three builds of #14304 on 25.4.4, 6 launches each: nothing 4254, engine on the launch thread with the background context 3554, no such engine with the background context 3541, background context deferred until started 4150.

## The cause

The first context of a JVM spends most of its time loading and initializing GraalPy's classes, about 10,000 of them, on the thread that starts the application. That is once per JVM, and the launch does other work for about a second before it gets there, so another thread can do it in that time.

- No context is needed for the effect: on another thread, only `Class.forName` over the same class list gives 3686 ms without initializing, and 3400 ms with, against 4058 ms with nothing and 3528 ms with a context.
- It is real work moved to another core, not work avoided: the same context on the launch thread first gives 4161 ms.
- The lead is what counts. A context started as the application's own starts saves nothing (4062 ms against 4092 ms): the application thread's CPU in its context falls from 2054 to 1475 ms, but its wall time stays at about 2100 ms, because the two threads wait for each other. Started when the context is configured, 3542 ms; at the start of `MicronautDevMain.launch`, 3281 ms against 4086 ms; from a `-javaagent` premain, 3107 ms.

`TruffleCompilerThread` stays at one thread with this. An `Engine` alone not helping also rules out language or option discovery and the context class loader of the first engine.

## The fix

`MicronautDevMain.launch` starts `PythonWarmUp`: a daemon thread that initializes a GraalPy context and closes it. Only a launch with Python sources starts it, or in test mode one with Python tests, on a JVM, with the Python runtime on the classpath and `micronaut.python.enabled` not false as a system property or environment variable. `micronaut.dev.python.warm-up=false` turns it off. Nothing is added at runtime call sites, and without a development runtime nothing changes.

## Measurements

The same jars in both columns, only `micronaut.dev.python.warm-up` differs, alternating, 8 launches each, medians, load average 3–5. CPU is the JVM's at `Startup completed`, then 1.5–3 s later.

| | Off | On | Saved | CPU at ready | CPU later |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| petclinic, 25.5.5 | 4039 ms | 3239 ms | 800 ms | 13.07 → 14.08 s | 15.39 → 15.63 s |
| petclinic, 25.4.4 | 4258 ms | 3389 ms | 869 ms | 14.16 → 15.08 s | 17.21 → 18.01 s |
| simple-python, 25.5.5 | 2714 ms | 2260 ms | 454 ms | 8.50 → 9.71 s | 11.50 → 12.76 s |
| simple-python, 25.4.4 | 2759 ms | 2285 ms | 474 ms | 8.71 → 9.94 s | 12.16 → 13.73 s |

The first request after ready doesn't change (petclinic 574 and 582 ms), so nothing is deferred to it.

Through the real `pyronaut dev` on petclinic and 25.5.5, 6 launches each: JVM start to ready 4186 → 3385 ms, the command to ready about 16.3 → 15.6 s. Reloads and the request after them are the same: 2526 and 2556 ms, 149 and 149 ms, 24 edits each.

With 12 busy loops beside it, load average 13–15: 6761 → 6098 ms. Held to the efficiency cores with `taskpolicy -c background`, 4 launches each: 27.2 → 23.5 s.

To have the two threads meet at different points, 90 launches started a probe context with the same options at a random delay up to 1.3 s, with no hang. That makes a class initialization deadlock unlikely, not impossible. With this change, a launch from an empty GraalPy resource cache works, 4 times out of 4.

## What it doesn't do

- **Configuration files.** It runs before the application's configuration is read, so `micronaut.python.enabled: false` in `application.yml` isn't seen. An application with Python sources that turns Python off that way pays the CPU of the warm-up, and nothing else changes.
- **`engine.CompilerThreads`.** The first engine of the JVM sizes the compiler queue (checked with thread dumps: 3 configured gave 3 without this, and 1 with it), and without the option the warm-up would give the default 4. An application that configures more than one gets one in development mode unless it turns the warm-up off. The guide says so.
- **Production.** A context started the same way also saves in `pyronaut run` on a JVM (petclinic 3916 → 3335 ms, simple-python 2687 → 2336 ms). This is left out on purpose: production must honour the two settings above and can't read them this early, and a production JVM can use the AOT cache below instead, though that was measured on the development launch only.

The AOT cache `tool.pyronaut.toolchain.aot-cache` already offers does the same job far better, and shows how much of this is class loading: the same petclinic development launch with a cache takes 1655 ms against 4086 ms in a separate series, CPU 7.56 s against 13 s, after a 12 s training launch. With a cache, a context started this way saves about another 150 ms (1504 ms). Reloads with a cache weren't measured.

## Tests

New `PythonWarmUpTest` in `test-suite-dev-python`: a Python launch warms up on a daemon thread with the launcher's loader and writes nothing, and a context works after it; Python tests warm up in test mode only; no Python sources, no runtime on the classpath, Python switched off and the off switch all start nothing.

Ran with `-Ppython-ci`: all of `:test-suite-dev-python:test` (22 tests, on the commit before the test mode addition), `PythonWarmUpTest` on the final commit, and all of `:micronaut-dev:test`, whose classpath has no polyglot. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-dev`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `test-suite-dev-python`; `micronaut-dev` has no enabled `checkstyleTest`. One run of `:micronaut-dev:test` beside other heavy work failed `DevRequestAdmissionTest` with a 403; it passed alone and in the next full run.

Not run: Windows, Linux, a native image, a machine with one or two CPUs, `pyronaut test -t` end to end. The measurements used this change laid over the jars of the test environment rather than a full build of this branch.

comment.body:
## Review

This is done carefully: both engines are closed and no reference to them is kept, the thread is a daemon with the parent loader as its context loader, it only runs from `MicronautDevMain.launch` on a JVM, and the off switch works through system properties.

1. **A class-initialization deadlock could hang the launch, with no way to recover** (`PythonWarmUp` around lines 77-81, `MicronautDevMain` line 144). The warm-up thread and the application thread run GraalPy/Truffle static initializers at the same time. If two classes depend on each other cyclically, the main thread blocks forever, with no error. The description calls it "unlikely, not impossible", based on 90 runs. `start` returns the `Thread`, but `launch` discards it. Your own numbers show that a warm-up started together with the application's context saves nothing, because the two threads end up waiting on each other. So having the application's Python context wait for the warm-up to finish (a latch or a published handle) should keep the ~800 ms lead and remove the deadlock risk.

2. **`engine.CompilerThreads` is overridden silently** (around lines 99-103). An application that sets `graalpy.engine.options.engine.CompilerThreads=4` gets 1 compiler thread in development mode, and only the guide says so. The warm-up already reads `micronaut.python.enabled` from system properties and the environment, so it could read that option the same way, or at least log at INFO when it sets the count. The reasoning in the comment is also unclear: the probe engine at line 117 is the JVM's first engine, built with default settings, yet the measured count was 1. This rule isn't documented and depends on the order in which engines are created, so it may break on a GraalPy upgrade.

3. **Initialization failures are logged only at DEBUG** (around lines 107-110). The `LinkageError` catch includes `ExceptionInInitializerError`. If a GraalPy static initializer fails on this thread, the class stays broken for the whole JVM. The application then gets `NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class …`, with the cause visible only at DEBUG. Logging non-`PolyglotException` failures at WARN would keep the comment's promise that the application's own context reports the problem.

issue.title: Development mode: read class files through a buffer in the dependency index
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

Every incremental Java compilation in development mode scans the class output with `ClassDependencyIndex`, which read each class file through an unbuffered `DataInputStream`. `DataInputStream` reads its stream a byte or a short at a time, so every field of a class file was a read from the file system: 109 reads for a 580-byte class.

## The fix

The class file goes through a 16 KB `BufferedInputStream`. Nothing else changes.

## In the stack

It conflicts with none of #14331, #14332 and #14333, and could land on its own on 5.3.x.

## Tests and numbers

- `ClassDependencyIndexTest` (new): a class file is read in at most 2 reads of the stream underneath (fails before the fix with 109 reads for 580 bytes), and a class file of several buffers is still read whole, with its constant field after the constant pool seen.
