issue.title: Keep the running generation in development mode while a configuration file cannot be read, and never exit the launcher over one
issue.body:
Part of #13654. Dev mode stays running after a failure and tries again on the next change, so the error can be corrected. A configuration file that could not be read lost the pool and, on the next start, could end the JVM.

## What was wrong

On petclinic in restart mode, with the Pyronaut command line kept out of the way, a syntax error in `application.toml`:

1. Failed the refresh, which restarted the application. The pool was released and Oracle went to 0 sessions, for a file no new generation could read either.
2. Failed the start of that generation in `Micronaut.start()`, which called `System.exit(1)`. The JVM stayed up about 30 s while its shutdown hook ran, then was gone.

## Cause

- `ConfigurationStaleness.refreshConfiguration` turned any failure of the refresh into "restart instead". A failed read leaves the environment as it was (`refreshProperties` publishes atomically), so there was no need.
- `Micronaut.mayExit` asks the environment whether it is in development mode. An environment that failed to read its files has published no properties, so it answers no, and the launcher exits. The setting `DevApplicationContextConfigurer` gave it is still among its property sources.

## The fix

- **The running generation carries on.** A refresh that fails, and whose environment can't be refreshed on its own either, gives `ConfigurationStaleness.UNREADABLE`. `DevRuntime` logs the error with what the parser says, leaves the generation running, and holds the batch as it holds one that failed to compile. Once the file is corrected, what waited is applied: a file put back as it was changes nothing.
- **The launcher no longer exits.** `Micronaut.isExitAllowed` also checks the environment's property sources for development mode, the one with the highest order deciding. This is reached only when `isDevelopmentMode()` says no, so a production start that fails exits as before.

The check in `DevRuntime` runs only when a configuration file changed. Nothing changes on any runtime path.

## Not changed

- A restart that was asked for still restarts, and a generation that already failed still tries a start, which fails until the file is corrected. The launcher stays up in both. In the second case the retained beans are released once the file is edited, as #14293 documents.
- A resource delivered in the same batch as the unreadable file is delivered again when the batch comes back. It needs a static file edited in the same batch; the batch has to be kept so that a later class change doesn't start a generation that can't read the file.

## Tests

In `DevRuntimeTest`. Each of the four failed before the change it covers:

| Test | Without the change |
|---|---|
| `aConfigurationFileThatCannotBeReadLeavesTheGenerationRunningUntilItIsCorrected` | Fails: a new generation |
| `aConfigurationFileCorrectedAsItWasLeavesTheGenerationAsItIs` | Fails: a new generation |
| `aStartThatCannotReadItsConfigurationLeavesTheLauncherUp` | The test JVM exits with 1 |
| `sourcesThatFailedToCompileStillWaitAfterAConfigurationFileThatCannotBeRead` | Fails: the first edit is lost |

- `:micronaut-dev:test`: passed in full before the last two commits (property order, sources kept). On the final code it had one failure, `whileNoGenerationRunsAConnectionIsAnswered503UntilAServerTakesTheSocketsBack`, whose client reached an SSH server on the port it had picked (`SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.9`). It passes alone. `DevRuntimeTest` passes on the final code.
- `MicronautDevelopmentModeSpec` and `TrainingRunTest` in `:micronaut-context:test` pass.
- `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-dev`, `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-context` pass.

End to end, with micronaut-projects/pyronaut#418, on petclinic with Oracle in restart mode: a syntax error in `application.toml`, then the fix, then an edit. Same JVM, Oracle container, pool identity and 2 sessions throughout, and requests kept answering 200.

Not run: YAML end to end (`DevRuntimeTest` uses JSON, since the TOML loader isn't in this repository), and the native toolchain.

comment.body:
## Review

The core behaviour is correct: `refreshProperties` puts back the old sources after a failed read, `lastResolved` doesn't move, the next good save refreshes in place, there's no reload loop, and the launcher still exits outside development mode.

1. **The held-back batch is never cleared when the fix is a resource-only edit** (`DevRuntime` lines 1483 and 1527). An unreadable read stores the batch in `failedBatch`. That batch is merged and cleared only by a later batch that has `full` set or contains sources (line 1483), and fixing the config file is a resource-only batch. The refresh then succeeds, but `failedBatch` stays set. Example: break `application.yml`, fix it, and an hour later edit a Java file. That batch is merged with the old one: the old config and static-resource changes go to the watches again, the configuration is refreshed again, and the old sources recompile. If the held batch had `full` set, a full rebuild is forced. `failedBatch` should be cleared, or applied, once the configuration reads again.

2. **The unreadable state isn't shown** (`ConfigurationStaleness` around line 447). Compile failures appear in the browser through `lastFailure`/`DevGateFilter` and in `DevEndpoint`; this state is only logged. A user who saves a broken TOML file and reloads the browser sees the old behaviour with no explanation, and every later class edit is silently held back. Also, the YAML parser's message doesn't name the file, because `AbstractPropertySourceLoader` only wraps `IOException`, so with several config files the log doesn't say which one failed.

3. **Unreadability is detected with a second refresh** (around lines 459-466). If `refresh()` reads the file successfully and moves `lastResolved`, then `apply()` throws while the editor rewrites the file and the second read fails, the result is `UNREADABLE` instead of a restart. The environment holds the new values but the beans were never rebound, and because the baseline moved, the next good save's diff leaves those keys out. The second read also re-reads every property source, so any failure anywhere is reported as an unreadable file.

4. **Scope:** "cannot be read" means parsing or I/O threw. An empty file, or a truncated one that is still valid YAML, is accepted and its keys are removed, which can lead to the restart and pool release this PR is meant to avoid. `settledResources` makes it unlikely, but it isn't prevented.

issue.title: Development mode: inject the LiveReload script into @View pages and other pages a body writer renders
issue.body:
Part of the development-mode reloading plan, micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654.

## Problem

Under `mnDev` and `mn:dev`, LiveReload's script was never injected into `@View` pages, so a browser showing a view did not reload on a change. Plain HTML pages, `String` or `byte[]` bodies and static files did get it.

## Cause

`LiveReloadScriptFilter` injects only into a body that is already text: a `CharSequence`, `byte[]` or a static file.

A view is not text yet when the filter sees it:
- Views' `ResponseBodySwapperFilter` replaces the controller's model with a `ModelAndView` and sets `text/html`.
- `RawModelAndViewMessageBodyHandler` renders the template into the response's stream when the response is written, after the filters.
- The filter therefore saw a `ModelAndView` and returned at its last `else`.

The same applies to any body a writer renders, such as a `Writable`. A route that only declares `produces = "text/html"` also has no content type at filter time, because the server sets it when it writes the response.

This was first read from the code, then confirmed by the new test, which fails without the fix: the `/view` page was served without the script. Views needs no change.

## Fix (development only)

When LiveReload injects its script and the response is HTML, the filter now does two new things:
- It renders a body of any other type with the writer the server would use for it, found in the `MessageBodyHandlerRegistry` by the body's class and the response's type. The render runs within the request's `ServerRequestContext`, as views' `writeTo` expects. The page goes out as rendered, with the script, so it is not rendered a second time.
- It takes the type a route produces when the response has none and the route produces exactly one. A route producing several negotiates as it writes, and is left alone.

A rendered page without a body end, or one the script must not go into, is sent byte for byte as its writer wrote it, with the writer's own type and no charset added. The writer writes against a copy of the headers. The response takes that copy only once the writer has finished, so a writer that gives up partway leaves the response as it was.

The response to a HEAD request is handled as the one to a GET: the body the route executor moved aside is handled, then put back aside. HEAD therefore gets the `Content-Length` of the page with the script and `Cache-Control: no-store`, as GET does.

The body end is found case-insensitively in the page itself, not in a lower-case copy, which can be longer than the page (`İ` becomes two characters).

### Content-Security-Policy

A page that declares a policy is left without the script, which the policy could block. Before this PR the filter already left alone a response with a `Content-Security-Policy` header, or with a policy in a `<meta http-equiv>` element. It now also covers:
- a writer that sets the header while it renders: the page is sent as rendered, without the script
- a policy added by a `ResponseHeaderPopulator`: the filter now runs ahead of `ResponseHeaderPopulatorFilter`, so it handles the response after that filter. Both had `FIRST.before()`, which left their order to how the beans were found.

The filter now runs at `ServerFilterPhase.FIRST.before() - 1`, ahead of the built-in phases and of views' filter, so it sees the response after them. A filter ordered ahead of it, such as one at `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE`, still sees the response after it.

Unchanged:
- With LiveReload off the filter returns at its first check, as before.
- A response that is not HTML (JSON, a CSS file) is untouched.
- The registry is resolved through a `BeanProvider` on the first page rendered.
- The filter is development-only, as before.

A blocking writer, such as views, now renders on the thread that runs the response filter rather than the one the server would choose for the write. This happens only in development mode with LiveReload on.

## Tests

`LiveReloadRenderedPageTest` (new, `micronaut-dev-livereload`) launches an application with:
- a model swapped for a page by a response filter and rendered by a blocking `MessageBodyWriter`, as views does
- a `Writable` route that produces `text/html`
- a JSON route and a CSS file
- writers that change their own headers while writing: one that sets an ISO-8859-1 charset, one that marks its output `text/plain`, one that sets a policy, and one that sets a header and then gives up with `UnsupportedOperationException`
- a writer emitting ISO-8859-1 with no charset and no body end

It checks that the pages carry the script with a matching `Content-Length` and `no-store`, and that HEAD gets the same length, type and cache header as GET. It also checks that the JSON, the CSS and the page without a body end are byte for byte as written, and that a header from a writer that gave up does not reach the response. It fails without the fix on `/view`. The HEAD, no-body-end and gave-up cases fail on the commit before review.

`LiveReloadScriptFilterTest` covers a page with `İ` before the body end.

`:micronaut-dev-livereload:test`, `:micronaut-dev:test --tests 'io.micronaut.dev.http.*'`, and `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on both modules pass.

## End to end

Java petclinic through `./gradlew mnDev` and `mvn mn:dev` on H2, with the sample's own build files and the jars of the earlier end-to-end test (core with #14275, #14307, #14328, #14329 and #14330; the plugin, module and serde #1500 PRs of that test, views #1212 and #1233 among them).

| Path | Without this PR, Gradle and Maven | With this PR, Gradle and Maven |
|---|---|---|
| `/vets`, `/vets/html` (`@View`, JTE) | no script | script, `Content-Length` of the page with it, `Cache-Control: no-store` |
| `/vets/json` | untouched | untouched, `application/json`, no cache header |
| `/resources/css/petclinic.css` | untouched | byte for byte the same, its own cache header |

The pages still carried the script after body, route, view, message and model edits, including after restarts. A first version without the filter order worked under Gradle but not under Maven: the views filter and this one had the same order, and the classpath decided which handled the response first. The order now makes the result independent of that.

## Codex

- Round 1:
  - A blocking writer ran on the event loop. Fixed: it now renders on the blocking executor, and the test's writer fails on an event loop.
  - A writer the response carries was ignored. Fixed: it is chosen as the server chooses it.
- Round 2: an `InputStream`, `File` or `ByteBody` HTML body turned into a 500, because its writer only writes through the server's response path. Fixed: such bodies are skipped, and the test covers a streamed page.
- Round 3: a writer that sets `Content-Encoding` while writing would be spliced into. Fixed: the page goes out as written.
- Round 4: the charset or type a writer sets while writing was ignored. Fixed: the page is decoded and sent with them.
- Round 5: a writer that marks its output as something other than HTML would be spliced into. Fixed: that output goes out as written.
- Round 6: a writer that sets a `Content-Security-Policy` while rendering still got the script. Fixed, and the test covers it; it failed before.
- Round 7: this filter and the response-header populator had the same order, so a policy the populator added might not be seen. Fixed by ordering this filter one ahead. A unit test of the order fails before; the end-to-end populator case passed either way, since the tie happened to fall the right way.
- Round 8 reports that a null stage from a `@ResponseFilter` declared to return `CompletionStage` is rejected. It is not: that check applies only to filters registered as functions (`RouteFunctionFilter`). An annotated method marked `@Nullable` may return null, and the JSON, CSS and synchronous HTML cases in the tests and on petclinic all ran through it.
- Rounds 4 and 5 are now covered by end-to-end tests of writers that change their headers while writing. Round 3, a writer that sets `Content-Encoding`, still has no end-to-end test. The petclinic e2e above ran before the round 5 change and was not rerun after review.
- After review: no findings.

comment.body:
## Review

The approach is sound and confined to development mode. Order −1250, the `@Nullable CompletionStage` return, unwrapping `CompletionException` on the blocking path, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding, and skipping encoded, CSP-protected and streamed bodies all check out.

1. **The script can be inserted at the wrong place** (`inject`, around lines 328-332). `lastIndexOf("</body>")` runs on `html.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`, and the original `html` is then cut at that index. Lowercasing can make the string longer: `İ` (U+0130) becomes `i̇`, two characters. On a page with N × `İ`, the script lands N characters before `</body>`, for example `…</d<script…>iv></body>`. The code already exists on `5.3.x`, but this PR sends every rendered view through it. Scanning the original string with `regionMatches(true, …)` fixes it.

2. **A page with no `</body>` is still changed** (around lines 249-256). When `injected == null`, the writer's bytes are still decoded and re-encoded through `replaceBody`, which also adds `;charset=…` to the content type. When neither the response nor the writer declares a charset, decoding assumes UTF-8. An htmx partial from a writer that emits ISO-8859-1 without a charset parameter then goes out as mojibake under `text/html;charset=UTF-8`, in development only. When nothing is injected, please send `out.toByteArray()` unchanged with the writer's own headers.

3. **HEAD requests aren't handled.** `RouteExecutor.finaliseResponse` moves the body into the `HEAD_BODY` attribute before filters run, so the filter returns early. HEAD then reports a Content-Length without the script, unlike GET, and lacks `Cache-Control: no-store`. The impact is small, but it contradicts the "matching Content-Length" claim.

4. **"Ahead of every other filter" holds only for filters ordered at or above −1250.** A filter at `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE` still sees the response after this one, so a CSP header or body it adds isn't taken into account. The Javadoc could say "ahead of the built-in phases".

5. **Minor:**
   - Every rendered HTML body is now fully buffered.
   - A writer that throws `UnsupportedOperationException` partway through may already have changed the headers, and those changes are kept.
   - As the description notes, there are no tests for a writer that changes its own headers while writing.

issue.title: A FSEvents run loop that cannot start no longer also reports that it ended
issue.body:
When the FSEvents run loop cannot start, the `FsEventStreams` constructor throws and closes the streams. The run loop thread could reach its end before the constructor closed them, and then also ran the callback that reports a run loop ending unexpectedly. `FsEventStreamsTest.aRunLoopThatCannotStartFailsTheConstructor` failed this way on CI, on 5.3.x and on PRs.

The callback now runs only for a run loop that started. A run loop that never starts is reported only by the constructor's exception.

The new test `aRunLoopThatCannotStartIsNeverReportedAsEnded` repeats the case 200 times; it failed locally on the 27th attempt before the change.

comment.body:
## Review

Looks correct. Before this change, the run loop thread could reach its `finally` before the constructor closed the streams. Now `started` is set only after `runLoop.complete(loop)`, so a run loop that never started is reported only by the constructor's exception. If the constructor gives up first (timeout or interrupt), it has already called `close()`, so `closed` is set and the callback still doesn't fire. The 200-iteration test reproduces the CI failure.

issue.title: Development mode: keep a bean whose recreation would stop the running application, and restart instead
issue.body:
Part of the development-mode reloading plan, micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654.

## Problem

`WatchableBeanContext.recreate` destroys a bean's transitive dependents before it creates the bean again. When one of those dependents is the running embedded server, destroying it stops the server, and stopping the default server stops the whole context. A module reloader that recreated a bean the server had received therefore ended the application.

micronaut-serialization#1500 found one case:
- Recreating `JsonMediaTypeCodec` destroys `MediaTypeCodecRegistry`, then `DefaultNettyEmbeddedServerFactory`, then `NettyEmbeddedServer`.
- On Java petclinic under `mnDev` and `mn:dev`, a body edit to a `@Serdeable` class with serde before #1500 stopped the run: the context stopped and Gradle reported BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
- The runtime still logged "generation 1 keeps running".

#1500 guards only serde's reloader. Any other reloader can do the same. The server's recorded dependencies include:
- the media type codecs
- `MessageSource` beans, through `CompositeMessageSource` and the HTML error response provider
- `HttpLocaleResolver`s
- the static resource and codec configurations
- the server configuration

The configuration refresher can hit it as well, when it destroys a removed `@EachProperty` entry that the server received.

## Behaviour chosen

The context keeps the bean, and the development runtime restarts the generation.

The context does not stop the application from under a reloader. It refuses the recreation, destroys nothing, keeps the running instances, and logs at INFO which bean it kept and which application bean recreating it would have destroyed.

Keeping the bean alone could serve a stale bean silently. So whenever the running generation had a recreation refused, the runtime restarts instead. A restart builds every bean from the new classes, and is slower than an in-place change but correct. This applies to:
- a redefinition, whose classes get their old bodies back first, so that requests finishing on the retiring generation run the bodies its kept beans were built with; resources patched with it get their old contents back, and the reloader is told of them again
- a resource patch, reverted the same way
- a resource change
- a configuration refresh the runtime runs for a changed configuration file
- a configuration refresh it does not run: the `/refresh` endpoint, or a configuration client's `RefreshEvent`. The restart is queued, not awaited, since the restart drains the request that refreshed.

Without a development runtime, for example in a test context with dependency tracking, `recreate` returns false and the caller keeps what it has, as it already does for a bean the context does not hold. A configuration refresh reports the beans it kept in `RefreshResult.kept()`, and `requiresRestart()` is true for them.

## Fix (development only)

All of it applies only where the context records the dependency graph, which only development mode does by default. Production paths are unchanged.

- `DefaultBeanContext.recreateBean` and `recreate(...)` refuse when the bean, or a dependent the context holds, is a running `ApplicationContextLifeCycle`. That is the interface for a bean whose stop stops the context: `EmbeddedApplication`, `EmbeddedServer`, Netty, and the servlet servers.
  - New `@Internal` method `tryRecreate(bean)` returns `Recreation.RECREATED`, `NOT_HELD` or `REFUSED`, so a caller learns what happened to its own call. `recreateBean` returns whether it was `RECREATED`.
  - New `@Internal` method `refuseStoppingApplication(definition, action)` does the check, the logging and the count.
  - New `@Internal` methods `refusedRecreations()` and `refusedRecreationsOnCurrentThread()` read the count, which only the development runtime reads.
- `BeanWatchRegistry`: a configuration watch that answered `RECREATE` for such a bean is told `REQUIRES_RESTART` instead of `IGNORED`. It decides from `tryRecreate`, so a refusal by another caller meanwhile, such as a `/refresh` on another thread, no longer turns a prototype's `IGNORED` into `REQUIRES_RESTART`.
- `DefaultConfigurationRefresher` keeps a removed `@EachProperty` entry when destroying it, with its dependents, would stop the application. A constructor-bound configuration whose recreation is refused is rebound in place for what setters and fields bind. Both are reported in the new `RefreshResult.kept()` rather than in `rebound()` or in neither list, and `requiresRestart()` includes them. `RefreshResult` is new in 5.3.0; the five-argument constructor stays.
- `InPlaceUpdates.restartRequired(context)` is true when the running generation's context refused a recreation since it started. It leaves out only what the listeners of the restart's own `ReloadCompletedEvent` refused on the runtime's thread: those beans were built from the new classes. A refusal before that event, or on another thread meanwhile, still counts. `DevRuntime` and `InPlaceUpdates` check it after:
  - the resource watches
  - the configuration refresh
  - the `ClassChangeEvent`
  - the `ReloadCompletedEvent`

  If it is true, they restart rather than report the change as applied in place. A redefinition or resource patch that becomes a restart is reverted, and is not counted as applied in place.
- New `KeptBeanRestarter` (dev): on a `ConfigurationRefreshedEvent`, when the context needs a restart, it queues a batch that changes nothing. The worker restarts if the generation it then runs still needs it, and does nothing if a batch restarted already.

## Which module reloaders could hit it

Read in the reloaders of micronaut-core#13654's modules, checked against the server's recorded dependencies:
- **serde** (#1465/#1473): yes. Recreating its lazy holders reaches the server through `JsonMediaTypeCodec`, `JsonStreamMediaTypeCodec` and `TextStreamCodec`, all three logged on petclinic. #1500 guards it there; with this PR the guard is also general.
- **None of the others recreates a bean the server received**: validation, cache, security, data (JDBC, R2DBC, Mongo, Cosmos), sql, views, flyway, kafka, rabbitmq, nats, jms, mqtt, mcp, langchain4j, servlet, r2dbc, and core's `DevRouter` and scheduler watch.
  - Filters, binders and body handlers reach the server through the router or are looked up at run time.
  - The validator, mappers and executors are held lazily or looked up.
- **Indirect cases.** Validation's, cache's and data's reloaders recreate interceptors. If an application bean the server received is advised by one of them, such as a `@Validated` or `@Transactional` `MessageSource`, it would be destroyed with them. These are now covered as well.
- **Core's refresher**: removing a `micronaut.router.static-resources.*` or `micronaut.codec.*` entry reaches the server. Covered here.

## Tests

All of these fail without the fix and pass with it:
- `RecreateRunningApplicationSpec` (inject-java):
  - recreating a bean a running server received, by instance and by type: before the fix the context stopped, with "Cannot resolve beans until the context is running"
  - recreating the server itself
  - a `RECREATE` configuration answer reported as `REQUIRES_RESTART`
  - recreation still working when the server is not running, or did not receive the bean
  - a prototype's `RECREATE` answer stays `IGNORED` though another caller had a recreation refused meanwhile: before, `REQUIRES_RESTART`
- `ConfigurationRefresherSpec` (context):
  - a removed `@EachProperty` entry the running server received stays, the application keeps running, and the result lists it in `kept()`: before, it was in neither list
  - a constructor-bound configuration the running server received keeps its value and is listed in `kept()`: before, it was reported in `rebound()`
- `RecreateRunningServerTest` (dev), against a real Netty server under the development runtime:
  - a class-change watch that recreates a `MessageSource`, on a body-only edit: before, the context stopped while the runtime logged "generation 1 keeps running"; now generation 2 starts and serves the edit, the retiring generation's controller runs its old body again, and no redefinition is counted (before: the new body, and one redefinition)
  - the same from a `ReloadCompletedEvent` listener: before, no restart happened
  - a configuration watch on the `MessageSource` answering `RECREATE`, for a `RefreshEvent` published on the test thread and then for `ConfigurationRefresher.refreshAll()`, as `/refresh` runs it: each starts the next generation; before, none did within a minute
- `RedefineWithResourcesTest` (dev): a redefinition with a resource patch that a refusal turns into a restart gives the retiring generation its old body and has the reloader apply the old resource: before, the new body and resource stayed
- `ResourcePatchInPlaceTest` (dev): the same for a resource-only patch
- `InPlaceUpdatesRestartedTest` (dev): a refusal by the restart's `ReloadCompletedEvent` listeners on the runtime's thread is left out; one from before that event, or from another thread during it, is not

Also run and passing:
- In full, on the final head: `:micronaut-inject:test` (758 tests), `:micronaut-inject-java:test` (6,392), `:micronaut-context:test` (265), `:micronaut-dev:test` (464) and `:micronaut-dev-tck:test` (6). Also `StaticResourceWatchSpec` and `SslKeyStoreWatchSpec` (http-server-netty), which read `RefreshResult.requiresRestart()`.
- `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on inject, inject-java, context and dev.
- `japiCmp --rerun` on inject and context, against 5.2.22: passes. `RefreshResult` and the new methods are new in 5.3.0. dev has no baseline yet.

`DevRuntime` is now 1,998 lines.

## End to end

Run before the fixes for the review, and not repeated since.

Java petclinic through `./gradlew mnDev` and `mvn mn:dev` on H2, with the sample's own build files and the jars of the earlier end-to-end test (core with #14275, #14307, #14328, #14329 and #14330; the plugin and module PRs of that test). To exercise core's guard on its own, serde was the build before #1500 (#1465 and #1473), whose reloader recreates `JsonMediaTypeCodec`.

A method-body edit to `Owner`, a `@Serdeable` entity, which compiles 54 sources and redefines 91 classes in place:

| | Gradle | Maven |
|---|---|---|
| Without this PR | the run ended: `Cannot resolve beans until the context is running`, the server's port closed, then `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` | the same |
| With this PR | three `Not recreating [...JsonMediaTypeCodec / JsonStreamMediaTypeCodec / TextStreamCodec]: it would destroy [NettyHttpServer]...`, then `Restarting:`; generation 2 served the edit in 4.9 s, a second edit in 7.7 s (100 sources compiled) | the same; served in 4.6 s |

With serde #1500, the same edit is redefined in place: Gradle 4.2 s, Maven 4.4 s. Other edits behaved as before: a body edit was served in 1.3 s, a route edit restarted in 1.4–1.6 s, a view edit in 0.1–0.35 s. Each run kept one process and port, and each was stopped cleanly.

## Codex

- Round 1: a recreation refused while a `ReloadCompletedEvent` listener runs was missed, because the count was only compared before that event. Fixed: the count is compared after it as well, and a test covers the case.
- Round 2: no findings.
- Rounds 3 to 8, on the fixes for the review:
  - The baseline taken after the restart's `ReloadCompletedEvent` also swallowed a refusal from a refresh as the new context started. Fixed: only refusals made during that event are left out.
  - That still swallowed a refusal on another thread during the event. Fixed: only refusals on the runtime's own thread are left out, counted per thread.
  - Reverting a redefinition left the resource reloader's patch applied, and a resource-only patch was not reverted at all. Fixed: the old contents go back into the generation, and the reloader is told of them again.
  - Last round: no findings.
  - Each fix has a test in `InPlaceUpdatesRestartedTest`, `RedefineWithResourcesTest` or `ResourcePatchInPlaceTest` that fails without it.

comment.body:
## Review

The core check is sound:
- **Production unchanged:** `refuseStoppingApplication` returns false without a dependency graph.
- **Detection:** it covers every running `EmbeddedApplication` and anything it transitively depends on.
- **No half-done destruction:** the check runs before anything is destroyed.

The weak part is how a refusal reaches the runtime.

1. **A refusal outside a batch the runtime drives never leads to a restart** (`DefaultConfigurationRefresher` around lines 282 and 313, `DevRuntime` around line 1525). The runtime notices a refusal only by comparing `refusedRecreations` before and after its own work. `RefreshEndpoint` calls `refreshAll()`/`refresh()` directly, and `applyEvent` handles `RefreshEvent`s from config clients. Example: in dev mode, `POST /refresh` after removing a `micronaut.codec.*` entry logs "running instances are kept until a restart". No restart comes, and the next batch takes a fresh baseline, so the outdated configuration stays until an unrelated restart. A refusal callback or event, or a sticky "restart pending" flag, would cover it.

2. **The counter isn't tied to the call that caused the refusal** (`BeanWatchRegistry` around line 540). It's one `AtomicLong` per context, compared around operations that don't share a lock. A `/refresh` refusal that happens during a configuration watch's `recreateBean` on a prototype turns that watch's `IGNORED` into `REQUIRES_RESTART`, and a batch can restart because of someone else's refusal. A three-state result from `recreateBean` (recreated / not held / refused) would be more reliable than inferring it from the counter.

3. **No revert when a refusal forces a restart** (`InPlaceUpdates.redefine`, around lines 200-207). When a reloader fails, `redefine` calls `revert(...)`, so requests finishing on the old generation run the old bodies. When `publishInPlace` returns false because of a refusal, it returns without reverting. In the petclinic case from the description, requests in flight during `beforeStop` run the redefined `Owner` bodies against the kept codec/serde beans, which is the mismatch the refusal exists to avoid. `redefinitions` and `inPlacePatches` have also already been incremented for what became a restart.

4. **Results are misreported without a dev runtime** (`DefaultConfigurationRefresher` around lines 282 and 313). A refused constructor-bound bean falls back to `refreshBean`, which can't change constructor-bound values, yet the bean is reported in `rebound`. A refused, removed `@EachProperty` entry is skipped and appears in neither list. The description acknowledges this, but `RefreshResult` should at least mark such beans as needing a restart.

issue.title: Development mode: serve an edited message bundle without a restart
issue.body:
Part of the development-mode reloading plan, micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654.

## Problem

Under `mnDev` and `mn:dev`, an edit to a message bundle (`messages*.properties`) was not served until the next restart. Nothing in the log said why. The development-mode guide says a changed message bundle reaches the beans that watch resources of its kind, but nothing watched them.

## Cause

- The build tools type the whole of `src/main/resources` as the configuration root. A bundle there is reported as a resource change of that root, and only a configuration file refreshes the configuration, so the change reached the resource watches and stopped there.
- No watch took it. The bundle is cached in three places:
  - `ResourceBundleMessageSource`'s message cache
  - its bundle cache, and its default bundle
  - the JDK's `ResourceBundle` cache, per class loader
- The generation's class loader reads the edited file live. But a generation keeps its loader, so the JDK cache kept the bundle it had already loaded.

## Fix (development only)

- `DevMessageBundles` is a `@Context` bean in `micronaut-dev`, active only in development mode. It watches the `.properties` files of every resource root (a `views` or `static` root nested in the configuration root takes the files under it). On a change, it:
  - clears the JDK's `ResourceBundle` cache of the generation's loader, whether or not the context has a message source, so code that calls `ResourceBundle.getBundle` itself (a view engine's resolver, user code) reads the edit too;
  - calls a new `@Internal` method, `ResourceBundleMessageSource.reload()`, on every `ResourceBundleMessageSource` the context created, of any scope. It records them as a `BeanCreatedEventListener<MessageSource>`, weakly, since a factory method may declare only `MessageSource`.
- `reload()` clears the JDK's cache for the source's class loaders, loads the default bundle again, and clears both caches. It runs with the generation's loader as the context loader.
- A source created with `new` rather than as a bean keeps its own caches; only the JDK's cache is cleared for it.
- The source is refreshed in place rather than recreated. Recreating it would destroy the composite message source and, through it, the server's HTML error response provider and the server, which stops the application. #14341 turns that into a restart; refreshing in place costs nothing.

Production behaviour does not change:
- Nothing calls `reload()` outside development mode.
- `getRawMessage` and the default lookup read the default bundle field once each, into a local, so a reload that empties it between two reads cannot fail a lookup. No synchronisation is added.
- The default bundle field is no longer `final`, since `reload()` replaces it. It is a plain field, not volatile, and nothing orders a lookup's read of it with the replacement: a lookup on another thread may use the previous bundle until it sees the write. The second reload 250 ms later drops what such a lookup cached, but nothing guarantees it is the last. The field's Javadoc says so.

## Tests

`MessageBundleReloadTest` (new, `micronaut-dev`) launches an application, edits `messages.properties` and then `messages_de.properties`, and checks each edit is served, with no restart and the same generation. Two cases:
- a controller reading a singleton and a `@Prototype` `ResourceBundleMessageSource("i18n.messages")`;
- a controller calling `ResourceBundle.getBundle` itself, with no message source bean.

Each fails without its part of the fix (`expected <200 hello-2> but was <200 hello-1>`): the first without the fix, or for the prototype with only the context's singletons reloaded; the second without the clearing of the generation loader's cache. With the fix, each edit is served within about a second.

`ResourceBundleMessageSourceReloadTest` (new, `micronaut-inject`) checks that `reload()` reads an edited bundle, and that a deleted default bundle leaves lookups empty.

Also run, all passing:
- `ConfigurationStalenessTest`, `DevRuntimeTest`
- after review: the whole `micronaut-dev` suite (458 tests, 1 skipped, 0 failures), and `micronaut-inject` `io.micronaut.context.i18n.*`
- test-suite `io.micronaut.context.i18n.*` and `io.micronaut.docs.i18n.*`
- `CompositeMessageSourceTest` (before review)
- `checkstyleMain`, `checkstyleTest` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-inject` and `micronaut-dev`

## End to end

The end-to-end numbers below predate the review changes; they were not measured again.

Java petclinic through `./gradlew mnDev` and `mvn mn:dev` on H2, with the sample's own build files and the jars of the earlier end-to-end test (core with #14275, #14307, #14328, #14329 and #14330; the plugin, module and serde #1500 PRs of that test). The edit changes `vet.ourVeterinarians` in `src/main/resources/i18n/messages.properties`, which the plugins type as the `i18n` root; the check is the heading of `/vets`.

| | Gradle | Maven |
|---|---|---|
| Without this PR | not served within 10 s (served only after a later restart) | the same |
| With this PR | served in 196–225 ms (median 207 ms, n=9) | 198–236 ms (median 212 ms, n=5) |

There was no restart and no new generation; the log shows `Message bundles read again: 1 message source(s) for 1 changed file(s)`. Edits made after the delayed second reload had emptied the caches were served in 6–15 ms, before the watcher fired, because the next lookup read the file. Body, route, view and model edits interleaved with these behaved as without this PR. The load average was 3 to 13. A view edit takes about 210 ms both with and without this PR.

## Codex

- First round: a lookup in flight across `reload()` can put back a value it read before the clear. This is fixed by a second reload 250 ms later, which keeps every lookup unsynchronised.
- Second round, the same point again: a lookup in flight for more than 250 ms, or one reading `defaultBundle` without a happens-before, could still keep a stale message until the next edit. Closing that completely would need a volatile field or a lock on `getRawMessage`, a production lookup path, which development-mode changes must not touch. It stays as described in `reload()`'s Javadoc.
- After review, three more: `defaultBundle` read twice could be emptied between the reads (fixed, read once); prototype-scoped sources were missed (fixed, every created source is recorded); bundles under nested `views` or `static` roots were not watched (fixed, every root is watched). The volatile point came up again and stays as above.

comment.body:
## Review

Sound and confined to development mode. `reload()` clears the JDK cache for both the generation loader and the inject jar's loader, the source's bundle cache and its message cache. That covers locale fallback chains (both `messages.properties` and `messages_fr.properties` edits), added or deleted bundles, and cached "not found" results. A lookup that races with a reload is fixed by the second reload 250 ms later.

1. **The Javadoc's ordering claim is wrong** (`ResourceBundleMessageSource` around lines 46-50). It says a lookup reads `defaultBundle` "after the cache's own synchronization". `getRawMessage` actually reads it at line 136, before `messageCache.get`, and a miss on a concurrent map gives no happens-before guarantee anyway. The description acknowledges the gap; the comment should say the same. Removing `final` also drops the final-field publication guarantee for production users, which is negligible in practice.

2. **Only bundles of `ResourceBundleMessageSource` beans are cleared** (`DevMessageBundles` around lines 73 and 88). Code that calls `ResourceBundle.getBundle` directly, such as view-engine message resolvers or user code, or a source created with `new`, gets nothing, and nothing is logged. Clearing the generation loader's JDK cache on every change, whether or not a bean exists, would cover these at no cost.

issue.title: Upgrade GraalPy and GraalVM to 25.5.5.0.3
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Moves GraalPy and GraalVM from 25.4.4.1.1 to 25.5.5.0.3, whose `python-resources` jar ships bytecode for the standard library. It had none before, so every GraalPy context compiled each standard library module it imported.

## What changed

- `managed-graal` and `managed-graalpy` in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`
- `graalVersion` and `graalpyVersion` in `gradle.properties`
- `version: '25.5'` for `setup-graalvm` in `python.yml` and `python-static-compilation.yml`. Oracle's download service lists "Oracle GraalVM 25 Innovation 5 25.5.5.0.3", and the action's version match accepts `25.5` for it
- the examples in `pythonRuntime.adoc`

`crema.yml` is left alone: it pins its own Oracle GraalVM for the Crema tests. Nothing else in the repository names the version.

## To decide before this leaves draft

- `python.yml` says it is synced from `micronaut-project-template`, whose `master` still has `version: '25.4'`. A sync would put it back, and the JDK would then no longer match the artifacts, so Python would run interpreted. The template needs the same change.
- `graalVersion` only feeds the docs, including `sdk install java {graalVersion}-graal`. SDKMAN lists Oracle GraalVM up to 25.4.4.1+1 today, so that command won't work until 25.5 is listed. `25.5.5+1` follows the old value's form and is a guess at the identifier.

## Is the shipped bytecode used?

Yes, checked on the embedding path as `GraalPyContextFactory` builds a context, with Oracle GraalVM 25.5.5.0.3 on the JVM:

- `sys.implementation.cache_tag` is `graalpy253-313`, the tag on the shipped files, as it is on 25.4.4. The magic number does change, `52530d0a` to `66530d0a`.
- All 681 shipped `.pyc` have flags 3: hash-based and checked. So extracting them, which changes modification times, doesn't invalidate them.
- `GraalPyResources` sets `python.CheckHashPycsMode=never`, so the hash isn't even computed. A plain context uses `default`; the hash there matched the source.
- With `python.VerboseFlag`, 69 code objects came from `.pyc` and 0 from source, in both a plain context and the virtual file system configuration.

The standalone launcher, a native image, also loaded `json` from `.pyc`. A native image of an application was not built.

## Measurements

Petclinic in restart mode on H2. Both lines use the same core and Pyronaut commits apart from the version, each with its own matching Oracle GraalVM JDK. 30 edits per series, first 10 discarded, medians of the other 20. The series alternate. CPU is per edit and includes about 3 s idle. `#14303` is lazy asyncio.

The cleanest round, load average 3–5:

| | reload | first request | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25.4.4 + #14303 | 1134 ms | 160 ms | 4.55 s |
| 25.5.5 without #14303 | 1090 ms | 161 ms | 4.13 s |
| 25.5.5 + #14303 | 1105 ms | 112 ms | 4.01 s |

Two earlier rounds ran at load 6–30 and are much noisier: reload 1172–1806 ms for 25.5.5 + #14303, against 1346–1564 ms for 25.4.4 + #14303, first request 113–214 ms against 194–210 ms. Differences of 50 ms in reload can't be told from noise here.

## Size

`python-resources` grows from 14.1 MB to 27.9 MB, and the extracted GraalPy home from 22 MB to 71 MB.

## Tests

With Oracle GraalVM 25.5.5.0.3 as `JAVA_HOME`, `./gradlew pythonCheck -Ppython-ci --continue`: every test passes except `NettyPythonEventLoopSemanticsTest.serverBindsEveryAddressOfAName`, which fails on macOS regardless of this change. `:micronaut-inject-python:compileVfsPythonBytecode` runs on the new JDK. That run was before the commit that only changes docs. No Java or Python source changed, so checkstyle and spotless have nothing new to look at and were not run.

Not run: Linux, Windows, this repository's CI (a draft runs none), `crema.yml`, a native image of an application, and tests outside `pythonCheck`.

comment.body:
## Review

The change is complete: CI is green, including the Python, static-compilation and native jobs, and nothing else in the repository still names 25.4 (`crema.yml` pins its own version, as the description says).

The PR is out of draft, but its description still lists two items "to decide before this leaves draft":
- `python.yml` is synced from `micronaut-project-template`, whose `master` still has `version: '25.4'`. The next sync would put it back, and Python would then run interpreted. The template needs the same change, before or together with this one.
- `graalVersion=25.5.5+1` is a guess at the SDKMAN identifier, and SDKMAN doesn't list 25.5 yet, so the `sdk install java {graalVersion}-graal` line in the docs won't work until it does.

Also worth a line in the release notes: `python-resources` grows from 14.1 MB to 27.9 MB, which every Python application picks up.

issue.title: Development mode: keep the annotation processors' class loader between Java compilations
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

javac closes the annotation processors' class loader when a compilation ends, so every edit compiled in development mode loaded Micronaut's processors and those of the modules again, verified them, and ran them interpreted until the JIT caught up: about 260 ms of every Java reload on java-petclinic, and most of the CPU of a body edit.

## The fix

`ProcessorLoaders` keeps the loader of a processor path between compilations of a `JavacSourceCompiler`, with javac's close at the end of a compilation left without effect. It loads them again when the path, or what it holds, changes: each file's identity, size, modification and change times, the regular files of a directory on the path, and the entries a jar's manifest names on its `Class-Path`. Any failed compilation that ran the processors leaves the loader unused afterwards: a processor may have thrown, or failed and been skipped by Micronaut's own error handling, its class left uninitializable, or the compilation may have stopped before the final round in which the processors release their state (`ANNOTATION_DEFAULTS` among it). `close()` and a discard stop keeping a loader, which closes once no compilation uses it.

The system property `micronaut.dev.compile.retain-processors=false` on the development JVM gives every compilation a loader of its own; the user guide documents it under *Compilers*. No processor is detected by name.

## Processors' static state

What a processor keeps in static fields stays with its classes, as in a build tool's daemon that keeps the loader. I checked what the processors in question keep (static fields of a mutable type or not final, read from the class files):

- **Micronaut's own** (core-processor, inject-java, and on java-petclinic's path data, serde, validation, security, sourcegen, graal): the per-compilation caches are cleared when a compilation ends (`BeanDefinitionWriter.finish()`), and what remains is constant tables and reflection handles. The visitors of `BeanElementVisitor.VISITORS` are a static, service-loaded list, so the same instances get `start` and `finish` on every compilation and keep any state of their own between them; `ProcessorLoaders`' Javadoc says so. The exception was the expression counter, which the pull request below this one fixes.
- **Lombok**: reflection handles, its shadow class loader, and a cache of `lombok.config` files that checks their modification times. Built to live in an IDE's long-running compiler.
- **MapStruct**: constant tables, and FreeMarker's template caches over templates in its own jar.
- **Micronaut OpenAPI 7.3.0: produces wrong output with a kept loader.** `Utils`, `SchemaDefinitionUtils`, `OperationUtils`, `OpenApiExtraSchemaVisitor` and others keep the document, schemas and groups of a compilation in static fields. `Utils.clean()` releases them, but nothing in OpenAPI's own processing calls it. #14284 showed the effect for Python (a renamed schema stays in the document). Until OpenAPI releases its state when a compilation ends, with #14294's `finishCompilation` the intended hook, its document in development mode can hold what an earlier compilation saw. micronaut-projects/micronaut-openapi#2877 fixes it. Meanwhile `micronaut.dev.compile.retain-processors=false` turns the kept loader off.

## In the stack

Built on the pull requests below it: `JavacSourceCompiler.java` conflicts with each of #14331, #14332 and #14333, `JavacSourceCompilerSpec.groovy` with #14331 and #14333, and the test processors' service file with #14332 and #14333. It also relies on #14333 running one embedded javac compilation at a time, so that two never share the processors' static state at once, and on #14336.

## Tests

New in `JavacSourceCompilerSpec`, with a test processor that counts in a static field how often its class was initialized:

- the loader is kept between compilations, and another compiler has its own (fails before: the count stays 1);
- a new path entry, a file added to a directory of the path, a file rewritten to the same size with its time set back, and a file added to a directory a jar's manifest names, each load the processors again; nothing changed keeps them;
- a processor that throws starts the next compilation over, and so does a source that fails to compile after the processors ran (fails before: the loader was kept);
- with `micronaut.dev.compile.retain-processors=false` each compilation loads the processors again;
- a loader discarded, or released by `close()`, while a compilation uses it closes only once that compilation returns it;
- a class with an evaluated expression compiled again keeps the name of its expression class (fails without the pull request below this one).

On java-petclinic with Gradle, the stack below → this: method body 725 → 425 ms (CPU 1243 → 475), route 1017 → 676, repository query 2210 → 1403, body in the entity 3261 → 2181, entity field 3562 → 2429; the CPU of an edit falls by 55-65%. The embedded compiler alone, warm, compiles a body edit in 161 ms with the loader kept against 450 ms without.

The whole table, from the same runs:

### Measurements on java-petclinic (8 Nov 2026)

Edit to served, in ms: the median of the last 4 of 6 edits of each kind per series, two or three series per variant alternated with the others, then p10-p90 and the CPU time of the development JVM per edit. Each edit was checked by a request; none went unserved (about 560 edits). Variants are cumulative: each adds one pull request of the stack to the one before. All carry the same modules, as the earlier java-petclinic runs' fixed variant, with the `DevelopmentSerdeReloader` prototype patch, without which the base variant hangs on its first compile-all (a serde reloader bug outside this stack). H2, machine shared, load is the 1-minute average.

`./gradlew mnDev`:

| Edit | base (#14331-#14333) | + #14334 | + #14335 | + #14336, #14337 | + #14338 | + #14339 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

The mechanism is sound, and invalidation is careful and well tested:
- The fingerprint covers file identity, size, mtime, `unix:ctime`, the files under a directory entry, and manifest `Class-Path` jars.
- Replaced loaders are closed, and loaders are not kept on Windows.

1. **There's no way to turn it off, though OpenAPI's output is known to go stale.** Keeping the loader depends only on the OS (`ProcessorLoaders` around line 67). Micronaut's processors catch many failures themselves: `TypeElementVisitorProcessor` ignores `Throwable` from supported annotation names and `NoClassDefFoundError`, turns a `Throwable` from `start` into a compile error, and `SoftServiceLoader` drops visitors it can't create. In those cases javac returns false and the loader is kept. Example: a third-party visitor's static initializer fails once during an edit. The class stays in the "Could not initialize class" state, and the visitor is skipped or errors on every compilation until dev mode restarts. Before this PR, the next compilation recovered. A related case: when javac stops without a final round, `BeanDefinitionWriter.finish()` doesn't run, and `ANNOTATION_DEFAULTS` can keep outdated defaults of a project annotation the user just edited. Discarding the loader after any failed compilation that ran processors would cover both. A failed compile already costs a recompile, so the reload is cheap.

**Smaller:**
- The description says the visitors are new for every compilation. `BeanElementVisitor.VISITORS` is a static, service-loaded list, so the same instances get `start`/`finish` on every compilation and keep any state between them. Please document that, or load `VISITORS` again for each compilation.
- `discard()` runs after the properties lock is released, and `DevRuntime.close()` closes the compiler after a timed join of the worker. If compilations ever overlapped, a loader could be closed while still in use. Compilations currently run on the single reload worker, so this is latent.

issue.title: Compile a new source with the sources of what processors aggregate from several sources
issue.body:
Part of stack #14340 (embedded compiler efficiency), on top of #14339. Tracked in #13654.

## Problem

The embedded compiler credits each processor output to the sources whose elements it came from (#14332). A source with no record in the index, such as a newly added one, shares nothing recorded with any other source, so it compiles alone.

A processor that aggregates from several sources writes its output again from the sources of that one compilation. OpenAPI is an example. When a new controller compiles alone, the round holds no `@OpenAPIDefinition` class. OpenAPI then uses the default title and version and writes a stray `META-INF/swagger/service-1.0.0.yml`. The real document is not rewritten, so it lacks the new endpoint. A processor that always writes the same file would replace it with the new source's contribution alone.

## Change

- A changed source the index has no record of compiles with every source credited with a class-output resource that two or more existing sources are credited with. The existing rule for shared outputs then applies as usual.
- For such a batch, the compiler skips #14338's attempt to compile the changed sources alone. A new source's classes are not in the output yet, so the structure check always fails and the attempt would be wasted.
- When the new source is compiled with those sources, it is not noted as having changed its structure. Otherwise its next body edit would compile its dependents for no reason.
- A compiled source that produced nothing, such as a `package-info.java` without annotations, now gets an empty record. Otherwise every edit to it would count as a new source.
- The rule depends on no processor by name. It does not apply to full compilations, or to a compiler whose processors keep state and rewrite their aggregates themselves (KSP, `compilesEmptyBatches`).

A deleted source needs no rule of its own. If it was credited with an aggregate, its other contributors already compile through the shared-output rule. If it was not, the aggregate does not depend on it.

## Cost

In an app with aggregate resources, adding a source recompiles those resources' contributors. In the test app with micronaut-projects/micronaut-openapi#2879, adding a controller compiles 6 sources instead of 1. With OpenAPI 7.3.0, which credits its document to nearly every class, it compiles 12 instead of 1. Other edits are unchanged.

## Tests

New specs in `JavacSourceCompilerSpec`, using the test `AggregatedProcessor`, which writes one resource and one source credited to every annotated class:

- **A new source compiles at once with the sources of the aggregate.** With `First` and `Second` aggregated, adding `Third` compiles all three and the resource holds `[First, Second, Third]`. Deleting `Second` then writes `[First, Third]`. A `CountedProcessor` count shows the new source compiled once, not alone first.
  - Fails on 09: only `Third.java` compiles, and the resource becomes `[Third]`.
  - Fails without the skip: the count is 5 instead of 4.
- **A new source compiles alone when no resource is credited to several sources.** Passes before and after; it guards the cost.
- **A new source compiled with an aggregate's sources compiles alone on its next body edit.**
  - Fails without the change that keeps a new source from being noted as changing its structure.
- **An edited `package-info.java` without annotations compiles alone.**
  - Fails without the empty record.

`:micronaut-dev:test` (552 tests, 1 skipped) and `:micronaut-dev-tck:test` (6 tests) pass in full. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` pass on `micronaut-dev`.

## Measured with the processor matrix

The harness drives `JavacSourceCompiler` directly on a 12-source app with Lombok, MapStruct, Immutables, Micronaut inject, Validation, Serde, Data JDBC and OpenAPI, through 21 edits. Each edit is compared with a fresh full compilation. Core here is this branch with #14294 merged locally. "Before" is a kept compiler on the 09 head (65f9c14990); "after" is a kept compiler on this branch.

**OpenAPI #2879 + #2877** (both merged locally):
- s20 (new controller) and s21 (mapper deleted) had 4 divergences before: `demo-1.yml` lacked `/health`, and a stray `service-1.0.0.yml` was written. After: none, in any step.
- s20 now compiles the new controller with `Application`, `Owner`, `OwnerController`, `PetController` and `PetResponse`, the document's contributors.
- s21 now also compiles `HealthController`, which is credited with the document.

| edit | s01 | s02 | s03 | s04 | s05 | s06 | s07 | s08 | s09 | s10 | s11 | s12 | s13 | s14 | s15 | s16 | s17 | s18 | s19 | s20 | s21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 1 | 6 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 6 | 7 | 7 | 6 | 12 | 9 | 1 | 5 | 9 | 9 | 7 | 1 | 6 |
| after | 1 | 6 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 6 | 7 | 7 | 6 | 12 | 9 | 1 | 5 | 9 | 9 | 7 | **6** | **7** |

**OpenAPI 7.3.0:**
- At s20 and s21 the stray `service-1.0.0.yml` is gone, and `demo-1.yml` has `/health`.
- `demo-1.yml` still differs from the full compilation from s08 on, before and after (`Animal_1`, a leftover `Address`). That is OpenAPI's static state surviving in the kept processor loader, which #2877 fixes.
- Sources compiled per edit: s01 to s19 are unchanged (11 each, 12 for s13). s20 goes from 1 to 12, s21 from 10 to 11.

## Known follow-ups (not in this PR)

- An existing source that starts contributing to an aggregate, for example one that gains `@Controller`, has a record, so it still compiles alone. OpenAPI still writes `service-1.0.0.yml` for it.
- A type that an edited controller references for the first time is read from its class file, so it loses its Javadoc in the document.

## Limitations and open review points

- Only class-output resources credited to two or more sources count as aggregates (Codex P1). Generated sources and classes credited to several sources are left out on purpose. A bean definition is credited to its superclass's source too, so counting those would make every new source compile each superclass/subclass pair. A processor that aggregates only into a generated source is therefore not covered.
- An aggregate with a single contributor is credited once, so it looks like an output of that source alone (Codex P1). Adding the second contributor compiles it alone, as before this change.
- The rule reads the index of the embedded compiler. When development mode starts over the build tool's output, the index has no records until sources compile here, and there are no shared resources to go on.
- Once some sources compiled here and the index holds shared resources, the index is partly recorded: a source only the build tool compiled has no record, so its first edit here counts as a new source's. It compiles with every source credited with an aggregate and skips #14338's alone attempt, once per such source. Telling it from a new source by its classes in the output was tried and dropped: its first edit here may be what makes it contribute to an aggregate, and compiling it alone would then drop the other contributions (Codex P1).
- Sources only the build tool compiled are not credited with an aggregate, so `sourcesOfSharedResources` misses them, and a rewrite can still drop their contributions. The shared-output rule has the same limit, so this is not a regression.


## Review follow-up (9 Nov 2026)

- The partly recorded index and the build-tool-only sources are listed above. Treating an unrecorded source whose inferred classes are in the output as not new was implemented and then reverted. Codex found it unsafe: when that source's first edit adds it to an aggregate, compiling it alone would rewrite the aggregate from it alone. So the cost stays as a first-edit cost and is listed.
- The redundant `request.deleted().contains(source)` check is gone.

Ran: `:micronaut-dev:test --tests 'io.micronaut.dev.compile.*'` and `'io.micronaut.dev.change.*'` with `DevManifestSpec` and `SiblingOutputTest`, `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on `micronaut-dev`, and the whole `:micronaut-dev:test` (577 tests, 1 skipped) and `:micronaut-dev-tck:test` (6) on this branch, none failing. Codex review: one P1 on the reverted change, none on the final one.

comment.body:
## Review

The logic is sound and works with the existing shared-output rule. The empty record for a compiled source that produced nothing, and skipping a new source in `learnStructure`, both do what they should. `classesOf` infers a class from the path for a source that isn't recorded, so an existing source the build tool compiled is still compared, not skipped as new. A few notes:

1. **The index can be partly recorded.** When development mode starts over the build tool's output, any source the embedded compiler hasn't compiled yet has no record, so `isRecorded` treats it as new. Once some sources have compiled here and the index holds shared resources, the first edit of each untouched source compiles every source credited with an aggregate and skips the alone attempt of #14338. The PR covers the empty index but not this partly recorded state.

2. **Aggregates can still be incomplete in that mode.** Sources only the build tool compiled aren't credited with the aggregate, so `sourcesOfSharedResources` misses them, and a rewrite can still drop their contributions. This isn't a regression, since the shared-output rule has the same limit, but it could be listed with the other limitations.

3. **Minor:** `request.deleted().contains(source)` in `aggregatingWithNewSources` compares index paths, which are normalized, with request paths that may not be. It's harmless, because the `Files.isRegularFile` check before it already excludes deleted files, so the condition is redundant.

issue.title: Name the class of an evaluated expression after the element that declares it, rather than numbering it
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

The classes generated for the evaluated expressions of a class were numbered (`$Foo$Expr0`, `$Foo$Expr1`, ...) by `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter`, a static map that is never cleared. In a JVM that keeps the processors' classes loaded between compilations, as a build tool's daemon does and as development mode will (the next pull request in this stack), a class compiled again gets new names: `$Foo$Expr1` instead of `$Foo$Expr0`. A new name is a class added and another removed, so development mode restarts the application where it could redefine the class in place, and compiling the changed source alone first (later in this stack) finds an output it does not have.

Numbers also depend on which sources a compilation holds. An expression is named after the class that declares the annotated element, so when `Bar extends Foo` compiles without `Foo`, the members `Bar` inherits number `$Foo$Expr<n>` from 0 and can overwrite a class `Foo`'s compilation wrote for another expression (constructors are not inherited, so the numbering shifts). `Foo`'s definition then evaluates the wrong expression.

## The fix

An expression class is named after what declares it, rather than numbered: the class declaring the annotated element, the element, the annotation and its member, and a hash.

```
test.$Foo$Expr$field$b$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$constructor$param0$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$method$find$param1$Value$value$<hash>
test.$Foo$Expr$type$Requires$condition$<hash>
```

- Each language describes the element (`getExpressionElementName`, a new internal hook of `AbstractAnnotationMetadataBuilder`): `type`, `field$<name>`, `property$<name>` (Kotlin, Groovy, Python), `getter$<name>` and `setter$<name>` (Kotlin), `component$<name>` (Java records), `method$<name>`, `constructor`, and a parameter by its index (`$param<n>`), which a class file keeps when it has no parameter names. Python, which always compiles from source, names a parameter.
- A Kotlin accessor and a setter's parameter belonged to `java.lang.Object` until now, since `getClassDeclaration` does not resolve them. Their expressions are now named in the class declaring the property.
- The hash, the first 64 bits of SHA-256 as 16 hexadecimal digits, covers the erased parameter types of a method or constructor, the annotation's package and the expression, so overloads, annotations of the same simple name and repeated annotations get names of their own, and a class of a given name holds the expression it was named for.
- Characters that cannot be in a Java name become `_`. A name longer than 200 bytes in UTF-8 is cut short before the hash, and so is the class's own name when it leaves no room.
- An element a language does not describe, such as an annotated type argument, is numbered as before, and `EvaluatedExpressionReferenceCounter` stays for that and for other modules that number their own expressions.

The name no longer depends on the other sources of the compilation or on the order elements are visited, so the classes need no reset between compilations.

When the annotated element is read from a class file (`isReadFromClassFile`, the other new hook), the compilation of its class wrote the expression class. `EvaluatedExpressionProcessor` then looks the class up and does not write it again when it is found. A subclass compiled on its own neither rewrites nor takes over the classes of its superclass. A superclass compiled by a version that numbered its expression classes has none of that name, and the subclass writes them as before. An element of a source of the compilation is always written, so a stale class file on the class path is never trusted.

Editing an expression changes its hash, so its class is renamed. Compiling a class whose expressions did not change keeps their names.

## In the stack

It touches no file of #14331, #14332 or #14333 and could land on its own on 5.3.x; #14337 relies on it.

## Tests

- `EvaluatedExpressionClassNamesSpec` (new, core-processor): the format, what goes into the hash, arrays whose values would join to the same text, expressions whose 32-bit hashes collide, replaced characters, and names cut short for long ASCII and CJK class and element names.
- `ExpressionClassNamesSpec` (inject-java):
  - the names of a field, a constructor parameter and a method parameter;
  - the same names when a class is compiled twice in one JVM;
  - distinct names for overloads with the same expression and for repeated `@Property` annotations, and 250-character and 100-CJK-character field names cut short to 200 bytes;
  - `Foo`, with an expression on a constructor parameter and one on a field, compiled on its own, then `Bar extends Foo` compiled on its own against `Foo`'s class files: `Bar`'s output holds no `$Foo$Expr` class, and both beans get the right values. Without the class-path lookup, this test fails;
  - with `Foo`'s expression classes removed, as from an older compilation, `Bar` writes the one it inherits.
- The Java and Groovy test helpers `AbstractEvaluatedExpressionsSpec` find the classes by name, not by the counter. The Kotlin `MethodArgumentEvaluationContextExpressionsSpec` checks the name of a function's expression class.
- Ran: `:micronaut-core-processor:test` (38), `:micronaut-inject-java:test` (6393, 10 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-groovy:test` (1342, 14 skipped), `:micronaut-inject-kotlin:test` (1111, 9 skipped), `:test-suite-jdt:test` (87, javac and JDT name the classes the same), and the `io.micronaut.docs.expressions` tests of `test-suite`, `test-suite-groovy` and `test-suite-kotlin`; none failed. `:test-suite-python:compileTestPython` compiles the Python expression docs with the new names; the Python test tasks were skipped in this build. `checkstyleMain` and `spotlessCheck` on every touched module (only the 6 TODO warnings already there).
- Codex review, five rounds: names bounded by bytes rather than characters, Kotlin accessors, array values encoded unambiguously, long class names, and a 64-bit hash instead of 32 bits, all fixed. The fifth round found nothing.

comment.body:
## Review

**Restarting the numbering at 0 can overwrite another class's expression class.**

`AbstractAnnotationMetadataBuilder.buildEvaluatedExpressionReference` names an expression class after `getOriginatingClassName(element)`, and `JavaAnnotationMetadataBuilder` resolves that to the type enclosing the annotated element, not the source being compiled. When `Bar extends Foo` compiles without `Foo`, `Bar`'s definition processes the members it inherits from `Foo`. Their expressions are numbered `$Foo$Expr<n>`, starting at 0 now that the counter is reset, and `WRITTEN_CLASSES` is reset too, so the class is written.

Example:
- `Foo` has `@Value("#{a}")` on a constructor parameter, which becomes `$Foo$Expr0`, and `@Value("#{b}")` on a field, which becomes `$Foo$Expr1`.
- Constructors are not inherited, so an edit to `Bar` alone writes a new `$Foo$Expr0` holding expression `b`.
- That overwrites `Foo`'s class, and `$Foo$Definition` then evaluates the wrong expression for its constructor argument.
- In development mode, the overwritten file is also credited to `Bar`, so a later recompile or deletion of `Bar` removes a class that `Foo`'s definition needs.

A fresh class loader already behaved this way. With this PR, warm Gradle daemons (production incremental builds) and #14337's kept loader behave the same way, where before they kept counting up and avoided the collision. A name that doesn't depend on which sources a compilation holds would fix it, or not generating expression classes for elements read from class files.

**Smaller:**
- The reset needs every registered compilation to finish. Every processor registers the compilation, but only `BeanDefinitionInjectProcessor`'s final round removes it. A compilation that aborts on a processor exception stays registered until its `Elements` object is garbage-collected, and until then numbering carries on. In the shared test JVM, that could make `ExpressionClassNamesSpec` flaky, depending on GC.
- The reset is only correct if `BeanDefinitionInjectProcessor` runs last in the final round. That holds for the service-file order, but nothing enforces it when a build lists processors explicitly.

issue.title: Development mode: compile the changed Java sources alone first, and their dependents only when their structure changed
issue.body:
Part of micronaut-projects/micronaut-core#13654. Part of the development mode compile stack: Stack #14340 on 5.3.x, bottom to top: #14331 → #14332 → #14333 → #14334 → #14335 → #14336 → #14337 → #14338 → #14339.

## What was wrong

An incremental Java compilation compiled the changed sources with every source that depends on them, directly or not, as the dependency index tells, and every source when a changed class declares a constant another class can read. An edit to the body of a method in a class many others use therefore compiled most of the application, although nothing the dependents compile against had changed.

## The fix

`JavacSourceCompiler` now compiles the changed sources alone first, with those that share an output with them, when the selection is larger. If that succeeds and every file it staged in the class output is there already, a class with the same structure and a resource with the same bytes, every generated source it staged exists already (its bytes are not compared, the classes compiled from it are), and every output those sources had is staged again, the result is promoted and the dependents do not compile. Otherwise nothing is promoted, and the changed sources compile again with their dependents, as before; a compilation error also goes this way, so that the dependents' errors are reported too.

The structure is `ClassStructure`'s, which development mode already uses to tell a body change it can redefine: every member, descriptor, signature, annotation, constant value, the nest, the inner classes, the record components, the permitted subclasses, the parameters' names and the static initializer, without the `Code` attributes. For this decision the line numbers and local variables of the static initializer are left out too, though its code stays: javac emits line numbers by default, so a line added above `private static final Logger LOG = ...` would otherwise count as a structure change. Redefinition still compares the whole static initializer through `ClassStructure`, unchanged, since the JVM would not run it again. The `InnerClasses` entries about other classes' nested classes are left out (`DependentStructure`): concatenating strings or making a lambda in a body adds one for `MethodHandles.Lookup`, which says nothing about the class. Its own nested classes, anonymous and local ones included, count.

A compilation alone that does not stand costs a compilation, so the compiler remembers which changed sources' last compilation changed their structure (a repository's queries and an entity's fields are edited again and again): the next edit of one compiles with its dependents at once, and that compilation tells from the staged classes whether the structure was kept this time, which lets the following edit try alone again. When the alone attempt of the same request was rejected for something the classes do not show (a resource a processor aggregates, a new generated source, an output no longer produced), that compilation keeps the mark, so such a source does not try alone on every edit. This only predicts; what compiles alone is always checked whole. Classes and resources the processors generate from a source they generated for a changed source (a builder sourcegen writes for an entity, then its introspection) count as the changed source's. Why a compilation alone did not stand is logged at debug level.

It applies to Java only (`comparesStructureFirst()`), not to Kotlin, which inlines the bodies of inline functions into their callers, nor to Groovy. It does not apply to a full compilation, a batch that deletes a source, one that another language's changes take part in, or one that compiles a source of another module of the build.

## What the class file does not hold

A source's comments and its annotations of source retention are not in its class file. A processor that reads those, or reads a method body through the `Trees` API, from the changed source while generating output for a dependent saw them before, since the changed source compiled with its dependents; now the dependent does not compile until its own structure-affecting change, so that output can lag. Processors that support Gradle's incremental annotation processing already must not depend on such information of other types, and Micronaut's read annotation metadata from class files. Output that a processor aggregates from several sources is written again from the changed sources alone, so it differs from the output's and the dependents compile. Codex flagged this as P1 and suggested turning the shortcut off whenever processors run; that would turn it off for every Micronaut application, so it stays, stated here.

The user guide now documents this limitation (4075fba77c), in the section "Annotation processors that read the source of another class" under *What a Change Does* in `src/main/docs/guide/devMode/devModeReload.adoc`. It covers which processors can be affected and the two workarounds: save the changed source and the dependent together so they compile in one batch, or clean and restart development mode.

## In the stack
